cards.name: Triangle inequality (and its reverse)
cards.lay: Going straight is never longer than taking a detour. In proofs: to bound the distance between two things, insert an intermediate object and bound each hop separately (“add and subtract”).
cards.st: For any norm \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) on a vector space and any \(x,y\): \[ {\lVert x+y\rVert} \le {\lVert x\rVert} + {\lVert y\rVert}, \qquad \bigl|\,{\lVert x\rVert}-{\lVert y\rVert}\,\bigr| \le {\lVert x-y\rVert}. \]
ver: Metric form: \(d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)\).
Finite sums / integrals: \({\lVert \sum_i x_i\rVert} \le \sum_i {\lVert x_i\rVert}\) and \(\bigl|\int f\bigr| \le \int |f|\).
Expectation form: \(|{\mathbb{E}} X| \le {\mathbb{E}}|X|\) (a special case of Jensen, Jensen's inequality).
Sup-norm form: \(|\sup_a f(a) - \sup_a g(a)| \le \sup_a |f(a)-g(a)|\) (see Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\)).
cards.det: The “add-and-subtract” trick is the single most common step in RL analysis. To compare an estimate \(\widehat V\) with \(V^\star\), insert something you understand, e.g. \(V^{\hat\pi}\): \[ |\widehat V - V^\star| \le |\widehat V - V^{\hat\pi}| + |V^{\hat\pi} - V^\star|. \] Each term is then handled by a different tool (concentration for the first, an optimality argument for the second). The reverse triangle inequality says norms are 1-Lipschitz, which is why norms of random vectors concentrate (see Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions).
cards.ex: If \({\lVert \widehat Q - Q^\star\rVert}_\infty \le {\varepsilon}\) and \(\pi\) is greedy w.r.t. \(\widehat Q\), then for every \(s\), \(Q^\star(s,\pi(s)) \ge \widehat Q(s,\pi(s)) - {\varepsilon} \ge \widehat Q(s,a^\star) - {\varepsilon} \ge Q^\star(s,a^\star) - 2{\varepsilon}\): two applications of the triangle inequality around \(\widehat Q\).
cards.use: Error decompositions (estimation error + approximation error + optimisation error), regret decompositions, bias–variance splits in non-stationary estimators (true mean at time \(t\) vs. average over a window).

cards.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
cards.lay: The inner product of two vectors is at most the product of their lengths. Correlation can never exceed 1. Its most useful RL incarnation: a sum of \(n\) terms is at most \(\sqrt{n}\) times the root of the sum of squares.
cards.st: In any inner-product space, \[ |{\langle x, y\rangle}| \le {\lVert x\rVert}\,{\lVert y\rVert}, \] with equality iff \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent.
ver: Sums: \(\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\bigr)^2 \le \bigl(\sum_i a_i^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_i b_i^2\bigr)\); with \(b_i=1\): \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \le \sqrt{n\sum_i a_i^2}\).
Expectations: \(|{\mathbb{E}}[XY]| \le \sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} X^2\,{\mathbb{E}} Y^2}\); covariance form \(|{\operatorname{Cov}}(X,Y)| \le \sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}} X\,{\operatorname{Var}} Y}\).

Weighted / matrix form: for \(A \succ 0\), \(|x^\top y| \le {\lVert x\rVert}_{A}{\lVert y\rVert}_{A^{-1}}\) where \({\lVert x\rVert}_A = \sqrt{x^\top A x}\). This is the key step in linear bandits (see Elliptical potential lemma).
Integrals: \(\bigl(\int fg\,{\mathrm{d}}\mu\bigr)^2 \le \int f^2{\mathrm{d}}\mu \int g^2{\mathrm{d}}\mu\).
Generalisation: Hölder's inequality Hölder's inequality with \(p=q=2\).
cards.det:
Proof idea. For any real \(t\), \(0 \le {\lVert x - t y\rVert}^2 = {\lVert x\rVert}^2 - 2t{\langle x, y\rangle} + t^2{\lVert y\rVert}^2\). A non-negative quadratic in \(t\) has non-positive discriminant: \(4{\langle x, y\rangle}^2 - 4{\lVert x\rVert}^2{\lVert y\rVert}^2 \le 0\).

The weighted form follows by applying the plain version to \(A^{1/2}x\) and \(A^{-1/2}y\). The “sum of \(n\) terms” version converts an \(\ell_1\)-type sum into an \(\ell_2\)-type sum at the cost of \(\sqrt{n}\) — this is precisely where \(\sqrt{T}\) regret rates come from.
cards.ex: Optimistic algorithms obtain regret \(\le \sum_{t=1}^T b_t\) where \(b_t\) is a confidence width. If you can show \(\sum_t b_t^2 \le C\log T\) (e.g. via Elliptical potential lemma), then Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\sum_t b_t \le \sqrt{T \sum_t b_t^2} \le \sqrt{C\,T\log T}\).
cards.use: Converting sums of bonuses into \(\sqrt{T}\) regret; bounding \(|\phi^\top(\hat\theta - \theta)|\) in linear MDPs/bandits; bounding \({\mathbb{E}}[XY]\) in importance-sampling variance; policy-gradient variance bounds; \(\sum_{s,a}\sqrt{N(s,a)} \le \sqrt{SA\,T}\) in tabular RL.

cards.name: AM–GM inequality
cards.lay: The average of non-negative numbers is at least their geometric mean. Practically: a product can be bounded by a sum, and \(2\sqrt{ab} \le a + b\) lets you “split” a square root of a product.
cards.st: For \(x_1,\dots,x_n \ge 0\), \[ \frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n} \;\ge\; \sqrt[n]{x_1 x_2\cdots x_n}, \] with equality iff all \(x_i\) are equal.
ver: Two terms: \(\sqrt{ab} \le \tfrac{a+b}{2}\), equivalently \(ab \le \tfrac{a^2+b^2}{2}\).
With a free parameter (“Peter–Paul”): \(ab \le \tfrac{\lambda}{2}a^2 + \tfrac{1}{2\lambda}b^2\) for all \(\lambda>0\) (see Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul)).
Weighted: \(\prod_i x_i^{w_i} \le \sum_i w_i x_i\) for weights \(w_i\ge 0\), \(\sum w_i=1\) (follows from concavity of \(\log\)).
Harmonic mean: \(\mathrm{HM} \le \mathrm{GM} \le \mathrm{AM} \le \mathrm{QM}\) (see Power-mean inequality & \(\ell_p\) norm comparisons).
cards.det:
Proof idea. \(\log\) is concave, so by Jensen Jensen's inequality \(\log\bigl(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum x_i\bigr) \ge \tfrac1n\sum\log x_i\); exponentiate.

The tuneable two-term version is the one you use most: whenever a bound looks like \(\sqrt{AB}\) and you want separate control of \(A\) and \(B\), write \(\sqrt{AB} \le \tfrac{\lambda A}{2} + \tfrac{B}{2\lambda}\) and optimise \(\lambda\) later.
cards.ex: Freedman/Bernstein-type bounds give \(|\hat\mu - \mu| \le \sqrt{2\sigma^2 L/n} + bL/n\). If \(\sigma^2 \le \mu\) (e.g. bounded non-negative variables), AM–GM gives \(\sqrt{2\mu L/n} \le \tfrac{\mu}{2} + \tfrac{L}{n}\), which yields multiplicative bounds like \(\hat\mu \ge \mu/2 - O(L/n)\).
cards.use: Balancing exploration vs. exploitation terms; tuning learning rates (minimise \(\tfrac{a}{\eta} + b\eta\) at \(\eta=\sqrt{a/b}\) giving \(2\sqrt{ab}\)); variance-aware (Bernstein) regret analyses; choosing block lengths in non-stationary bandits.

cards.name: Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul)
cards.lay: A product of two numbers is bounded by a sum of powers. It is the cleanest way to “decouple” a cross term \(ab\) into a part depending only on \(a\) and a part depending only on \(b\), with a knob to trade weight between them.
cards.st: For \(a,b\ge0\) and conjugate exponents \(p,q>1\) with \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q = 1\), \[ ab \le \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}. \]
ver: Peter–Paul (\(p=q=2\) with a parameter): \(ab \le \tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{2}a^2 + \tfrac{1}{2{\varepsilon}}b^2\) for every \({\varepsilon}>0\).

Inner-product form: \({\langle x, y\rangle} \le \tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{2}{\lVert x\rVert}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2{\varepsilon}}{\lVert y\rVert}_*^2\) (with dual norm \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_*\)); central in mirror-descent analyses Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma.
Fenchel–Young: \({\langle x, y\rangle} \le f(x) + f^*(y)\) for any convex \(f\) with conjugate \(f^*\) Convex conjugate & Fenchel–Young; Young is the case \(f(a)=a^p/p\).
Convolution version (Young for \(L^p\) norms): \({\lVert f*g\rVert}_r \le {\lVert f\rVert}_p{\lVert g\rVert}_q\) with \(1+\tfrac1r=\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q\) (rarely needed in RL).
cards.det:
Proof idea. By concavity of \(\log\): \(\log(ab) = \tfrac1p\log a^p + \tfrac1q\log b^q \le \log\bigl(\tfrac{a^p}{p} + \tfrac{b^q}{q}\bigr)\).

The inner-product form with a dual norm is ubiquitous in online learning: the term \({\langle g_t, x_t - x_{t+1}\rangle}\) is bounded by \(\tfrac{\eta}{2}{\lVert g_t\rVert}_*^2 + \tfrac{1}{2\eta}{\lVert x_t-x_{t+1}\rVert}^2\) and the second piece is cancelled by strong convexity of the regulariser.
cards.ex: In a stability argument you may face \(2{\langle abla f(x), \xi angle} \) with noise \(\xi\). Peter–Paul gives \(2{\langle abla f(x), \xi angle} \le frac12{\lVert abla f(x) Vert}^2 + 2{\lVert \xi Vert}^2\), letting you absorb half of a progress term \(-{\lVert abla f Vert}^2\) and pay only for the noise.
cards.use: Online mirror descent and FTRL regret proofs; SGD and TD-learning convergence (absorbing cross terms); EM contraction arguments with sample noise; proving Hölder Hölder's inequality.

cards.name: Hölder's inequality
cards.lay: The generalisation of Cauchy–Schwarz to mismatched “sizes”: if you measure one function in an \(L^p\) way, you must measure the other in the dual \(L^q\) way. In RL, the most common use is \(|{\mathbb{E}}_P f| \le {\lVert P\rVert}_1{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty\).
cards.st: For \(p,q\in[1,\infty]\) with \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1\), \[ \Bigl|\sum_i x_i y_i\Bigr| \le {\lVert x\rVert}_p\,{\lVert y\rVert}_q, \qquad \int |fg|\,{\mathrm{d}}\mu \le {\lVert f\rVert}_{L^p(\mu)}{\lVert g\rVert}_{L^q(\mu)}. \]
ver: \(\ell_1\)–\(\ell_\infty\) (most used in RL): \(|{\langle p-q, V\rangle}| \le {\lVert p-q\rVert}_1\,{\lVert V\rVert}_\infty\). With probability vectors and a centred \(V\): \(|{\langle p-q, V\rangle}| \le \tfrac12{\lVert p-q\rVert}_1\,{\operatorname{sp}}(V)\) where \({\operatorname{sp}}(V)=\max V-\min V\).
Expectation form: \({\mathbb{E}}|XY| \le ({\mathbb{E}}|X|^p)^{1/p}({\mathbb{E}}|Y|^q)^{1/q}\).
Dual norm characterisation: \({\lVert x\rVert}_p = \sup_{{\lVert y\rVert}_q\le1}{\langle x, y\rangle}\).
Generalised (three functions): \({\lVert fgh\rVert}_1 \le {\lVert f\rVert}_p{\lVert g\rVert}_q{\lVert h\rVert}_r\) with \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q+\tfrac1r=1\).
Interpolation (Lyapunov): \({\lVert x\rVert}_r \le {\lVert x\rVert}_p^{\theta}{\lVert x\rVert}_q^{1-\theta}\) for \(\tfrac1r = \tfrac{\theta}{p}+\tfrac{1-\theta}{q}\).
cards.det:
Proof idea. Normalise so \({\lVert x\rVert}_p = {\lVert y\rVert}_q = 1\); apply Young Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul) termwise: \(|x_iy_i| \le |x_i|^p/p + |y_i|^q/q\), sum to get \(\le 1\).

The span refinement is important: since \({\langle p-q, c{\mathbf{1}}\rangle}=0\) for probability vectors, you may shift \(V\) by any constant before applying Hölder, giving \(\tfrac12{\lVert p-q\rVert}_1{\operatorname{sp}}(V)\). In discounted MDPs \({\operatorname{sp}}(V)\le 1/(1-\gamma)\); in average-reward MDPs \({\operatorname{sp}}(h)\le D\) (diameter), which is why bias span appears in regret bounds.
cards.ex: Simulation lemma step: \(|(\widehat P(\cdot|s,a) - P(\cdot|s,a))^\top V| \le {\lVert \widehat P(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\rVert}_1{\lVert V\rVert}_\infty \le {\lVert \widehat P - P\rVert}_{1}\cdot\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\). Combined with the \(\ell_1\)-deviation bound \(\ell_1\) deviation of the empirical distribution (Weissman et al.) this gives the classical \(\sqrt{S}\) factor in model-based RL.
cards.use: Model-error propagation (simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error)); TV bounds on expectation differences Total variation distance; mismatched norms in importance sampling (\({\lVert w\rVert}_\infty\) vs. \({\lVert f\rVert}_1\)); concentrability coefficients in offline RL.

cards.name: Exponential bounds: \(1+x\le e^x\) and friends
cards.lay: The exponential function lies above its tangent line at zero. This turns products into sums (via \(\prod(1+x_i) \le e^{\sum x_i}\)) and is behind almost every “\((1-{\varepsilon})^n \le e^{-{\varepsilon} n}\)” step.
cards.st: For all real \(x\): \[ 1 + x \le e^x. \] Consequently, for \(x\in[0,1]\) and \(n\ge0\): \((1-x)^n \le e^{-nx}\).
ver: Quadratic upper bound: \(e^x \le 1 + x + x^2\) for \(x\le 1\) (used for exponential weights / EXP3 Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound).
Lower bound near zero: \(1 - x \ge e^{-x - x^2}\) for \(x\in[0,\tfrac12]\).

Discount factor form: \(\gamma^H = (1-(1-\gamma))^H \le e^{-(1-\gamma)H}\), so \(\gamma^H\le{\varepsilon}\) once \(H \ge \tfrac{\log(1/{\varepsilon})}{1-\gamma}\) (see Geometric series & discounted sums).
Product form: \(\prod_i(1+x_i) \le \exp(\sum_i x_i)\); for \(x_i\in[0,1]\) also \(\prod_i(1+x_i) \ge 1+\sum_i x_i\).

\(\left(1+\tfrac{x}{n}\right)^n \le e^x\) and \(\left(1+\tfrac{1}{H}\right)^H \le e\) — the second shows up in finite-horizon UCB-style analyses (e.g. \((1+1/H)^H\le e\) in Q-learning with UCB bonuses).
cards.det:
Proof. \(f(x) = e^x - 1 - x\) has \(f(0)=0\), \(f'(x)=e^x - 1\) which is negative for \(x<0\), positive for \(x>0\), so \(0\) is a global minimum. Equivalently: \(e^x\) is convex and \(1+x\) is its tangent at \(0\).

The quadratic bound \(e^x\le1+x+x^2\) (\(x\le1\)) follows from the Taylor series: \(\sum_{k\ge2}x^k/k! \le x^2(e-2) \le x^2\) for \(|x|\le1\), plus a separate check for \(x<-1\).
cards.ex: Probability that \(n\) independent trials, each with success probability \(p\), all fail: \((1-p)^n \le e^{-pn}\). To make this \(\le\delta\) you need \(n \ge \tfrac{1}{p}\log\tfrac1\delta\) — the basic “coupon” sample-complexity calculation for reaching rarely visited states.
cards.use: Effective horizon computations; exponential-weights (Hedge, EXP3) regret proofs; Chernoff bounds Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method; analysing \((1-\alpha)^t\) contraction of stochastic-approximation iterates; learning-rate schedules \(\alpha_t = (H+1)/(H+t)\) in Q-learning.

cards.name: Logarithm bounds
cards.lay: Simple sandwiches for \(\log(1+x)\): it is close to \(x\) for small \(x\) but always below it. These convert multiplicative statements into additive ones and back.
ver: Second-order: \(x - \tfrac{x^2}{2} \le \log(1+x) \le x - \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^3}{3}\) for \(x\ge0\); and \(\log(1+x) \ge x - x^2\) for \(x\ge -\tfrac12\).
\(\log x \le x - 1\) for \(x>0\) — the key step in proving Gibbs' inequality \({\mathrm{KL}}\ge0\) KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality.
\(\log(1/(1-x)) \ge x\) and, for \(x\in[0,\tfrac12]\), \(\log\tfrac{1}{1-x} \le x + x^2\).
\(\log x \le \tfrac{x^{a}}{a}\) for \(a>0\) (log grows slower than any power) — used to absorb logs, e.g. \(\log T \le \sqrt{T}\).
Concavity: \(\log\sum_i w_ix_i \ge \sum_i w_i \log x_i\) (Jensen Jensen's inequality).
cards.det:
All follow from concavity of \(\log\) and comparing derivatives at \(0\): e.g. \(g(x) = x - \log(1+x)\) has \(g(0)=0\) and \(g'(x) = x/(1+x)\), which has the sign of \(x\), so \(g\ge0\).

These bounds are the bridge between “additive” and “multiplicative” worlds: e.g. the potential \(\log\det\) in Elliptical potential lemma uses \(\min(1,u) \le 2\log(1+u)\) for \(u\ge0\).
cards.ex: Elliptical potential: since \(\log(1+u) \ge u/2\) for \(u\in[0,1]\), \(\sum_t \min(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}) \le 2\sum_t\log(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}) = 2\log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\).
cards.use: Proving \({\mathrm{KL}}\ge0\); elliptical potential lemma; Hedge analysis (potential \(\log W_t\)); converting \(\log(1/(1-\gamma))\) terms; bounding \(\log\tfrac{1}{\delta}\)-type quantities.

cards.name: Geometric series & discounted sums
cards.lay: Sums of powers of \(\gamma<1\) add up to \(1/(1-\gamma)\). This single fact is why \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) is the “effective horizon” and why it appears everywhere in discounted-RL bounds.
cards.st: For \(|\gamma|<1\): \[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t = \frac{1}{1-\gamma}, \qquad \sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t = \frac{1-\gamma^H}{1-\gamma}, \qquad \sum_{t=0}^\infty t\gamma^t = \frac{\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}. \]
ver: Values are bounded: rewards in \([0,1]\) give \(0 \le V^\pi \le \tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\).
Tail: \(\sum_{t\ge H}\gamma^t = \tfrac{\gamma^H}{1-\gamma}\); truncating at \(H = \lceil\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\log\tfrac{1}{{\varepsilon}(1-\gamma)}\rceil\) loses at most \({\varepsilon}\) in value.
Second moment: \(\sum_t t^2\gamma^t = \tfrac{\gamma(1+\gamma)}{(1-\gamma)^3}\).
Matrix version (Neumann series): \(\sum_t (\gamma P)^t = (I-\gamma P)^{-1}\) Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\).
Inhomogeneous recursion: if \(e_{k+1} \le \gamma e_k + c\) then \(e_k \le \gamma^k e_0 + \tfrac{c}{1-\gamma}\).
cards.det:
Proof. \((1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t = 1-\gamma^H\) (telescoping Telescoping sums). Differentiate \(\sum\gamma^t = (1-\gamma)^{-1}\) in \(\gamma\) to get the \(t\gamma^t\) sum.

The recursion form is the template for every “approximate dynamic programming” result: an iterative scheme that contracts by \(\gamma\) but incurs error \(c\) per step converges to within \(c/(1-\gamma)\) of the target.
cards.ex: Approximate value iteration with per-step error \({\lVert V_{k+1}-TV_k\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\): \({\lVert V_k - V^\star\rVert}_\infty \le \gamma{\lVert V_{k-1}-V^\star\rVert}_\infty + {\varepsilon}\), hence \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty \le \gamma^k{\lVert V_0-V^\star\rVert}_\infty + \tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\).
cards.use: Every discounted analysis; effective horizon truncation; error propagation in AVI/API; normalisation of occupancy measures Discounted occupancy measures; computing expected trajectory length under geometric termination.

cards.name: Telescoping sums
cards.lay: In \(\sum (a_{t+1}-a_t)\) everything cancels except the ends. Many deep-looking RL identities (performance difference, simulation lemma, regret of potential-based algorithms) are telescoping sums in disguise.
cards.st: For any sequence \((a_t)\): \[ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(a_{t+1}-a_t) = a_T - a_0. \]
ver: Products: \(\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\tfrac{a_{t+1}}{a_t} = \tfrac{a_T}{a_0}\); take logs to telescope (used in potential-based Hedge proofs Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound).

Discounted telescoping: \(\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\bigl(\gamma f(s_{t+1}) - f(s_t)\bigr) = -f(s_0)\) (if bounded), the identity behind the performance difference lemma Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford).
Matrix/operator telescoping: \(A^n - B^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A^{k}(A-B)B^{n-1-k}\) — used for comparing \(n\)-step transition matrices.
Potential functions: if \(\Phi_{t+1} - \Phi_t \le -c_t + d_t\) then \(\sum_t c_t \le \Phi_0 - \Phi_T + \sum_t d_t\) — the skeleton of most online-learning and optimisation proofs.
cards.det: Telescoping is less a theorem than a proof technique: \emph{find the right sequence \(a_t\)}. In RL the clever choices are \(a_t = \gamma^t V^{\pi'}(s_t)\) along a trajectory of \(\pi\) (performance difference), \(a_h = {\mathbb{E}}[V_h^{\widehat M}(s_h)]\) under the true model (simulation lemma), and \(a_t = \tfrac{1}{2\eta}{\lVert x_t-x^\star\rVert}^2\) (gradient descent).
cards.ex: Gradient descent with step \(\eta\) on convex \(f\): \({\lVert x_{t+1}-x^\star\rVert}^2 = {\lVert x_t - x^\star\rVert}^2 - 2\eta{\langle g_t, x_t-x^\star\rangle} + \eta^2{\lVert g_t\rVert}^2\). Rearranging and telescoping over \(t\) gives \(\sum_t (f(x_t)-f(x^\star)) \le \tfrac{{\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert}^2}{2\eta} + \tfrac{\eta}{2}\sum_t{\lVert g_t\rVert}^2\).
cards.use: Performance difference lemma, simulation lemma, value-difference decompositions, regret of OGD/OMD, Lyapunov-drift arguments in stochastic approximation, Hedge potential analysis.

cards.name: Sums of \(1/\sqrt{t}\), harmonic sums & integral comparison
cards.plain: Sums of 1/√t, harmonic sums & integral comparison
cards.lay: Sums like \(\sum 1/\sqrt{t}\) or \(\sum 1/t\) behave like the corresponding integrals. These two facts produce essentially every \(\sqrt{T}\) and \(\log T\) in regret bounds.
cards.st: For \(T\ge1\): \[ \sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} \le 2\sqrt{T}, \qquad \sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{t} \le 1 + \log T. \] More generally, for non-increasing \(f\ge0\): \(\int_1^{T+1}f(x)\,{\mathrm{d}} x \le \sum_{t=1}^T f(t) \le f(1) + \int_1^T f(x)\,{\mathrm{d}} x\).
ver: Counts (pigeonhole) form: if \(n_t(k)\) counts visits to item \(k\) before time \(t\), then \(\sum_{t=1}^T \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{\max(1,n_t(k_t))}} \le K + 2\sqrt{KT}\) (via Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality); see Pigeonhole / count-summation lemma (tabular RL).
Power sums: \(\sum_{t=1}^T t^{-\alpha} \le \tfrac{T^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}\) for \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); \(\le \tfrac{\alpha}{\alpha-1}\) for \(\alpha>1\).
\(\sum_{t=1}^T\sqrt{t} \le \tfrac23(T+1)^{3/2}\); \(\sum_{t=1}^T\tfrac{\log(1+t)}{\sqrt{t}} \le 2\sqrt{T}\log(1+T)\) (pull the monotone log out).
Harmonic numbers: \(\log(T+1) \le H_T \le 1+\log T\); \(H_T = \log T + \gamma_{\mathrm{EM}} + O(1/T)\).
cards.det:
Proof. For non-increasing \(f\), \(f(t) \le \int_{t-1}^{t}f(x){\mathrm{d}} x\), so \(\sum_{t=2}^T f(t) \le \int_1^T f\). For \(f(x)=x^{-1/2}\): \(\sum_{t=1}^T t^{-1/2} \le 1 + 2\sqrt T - 2 \le 2\sqrt T\).

A slick alternative: \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt t} \le \tfrac{2}{\sqrt t + \sqrt{t-1}} = 2(\sqrt t - \sqrt{t-1})\), which telescopes Telescoping sums.
cards.ex: Online gradient descent with \(\eta_t = D/(G\sqrt{t})\) has regret \(\le \tfrac{D^2}{2\eta_T} + \tfrac{G^2}{2}\sum_t\eta_t \le \tfrac{DG\sqrt T}{2} + DG\sqrt{T} = \tfrac32 DG\sqrt{T}\).
cards.use: UCB regret (\(\sum_t\sqrt{\log T/n}\)), tabular RL bonuses, step-size schedules in SGD/stochastic approximation, anytime algorithms, doubling-trick costs Doubling trick.

cards.name: Minkowski's inequality
cards.lay: The triangle inequality for \(L^p\) norms: the \(p\)-norm of a sum is at most the sum of the \(p\)-norms. Use it when you need to split a moment like \(({\mathbb{E}}|X+Y|^p)^{1/p}\).
cards.st: For \(p\in[1,\infty]\), \[ {\lVert f+g\rVert}_p \le {\lVert f\rVert}_p + {\lVert g\rVert}_p. \]
ver: Moments: \(({\mathbb{E}}|X+Y|^p)^{1/p} \le ({\mathbb{E}}|X|^p)^{1/p} + ({\mathbb{E}}|Y|^p)^{1/p}\); for \(p=2\) the standard-deviation triangle inequality \(\sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}}(X+Y)} \le \sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}} X} + \sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}} Y}\).
Integral (continuous) Minkowski: \(\bigl\|\int F(\cdot,y)\,{\mathrm{d}} y\bigr\|_p \le \int {\lVert F(\cdot,y)\rVert}_p\,{\mathrm{d}} y\).
Reverse direction for \(0<p<1\) (not a norm): \({\lVert f+g\rVert}_p \ge {\lVert f\rVert}_p+{\lVert g\rVert}_p\) for non-negative \(f,g\).
cards.det:
Proof idea. Write \(|f+g|^p \le |f||f+g|^{p-1} + |g||f+g|^{p-1}\) and apply Hölder Hölder's inequality to each term with exponents \(p\) and \(p/(p-1)\).

The standard-deviation triangle inequality is very handy in variance analyses: it is how one shows that the “total variance” of a return is controlled by per-step variances in law-of-total-variance arguments Law of total variance (and the variance of returns).
cards.ex: If \(\widehat V = V + B + N\) (truth + bias + noise) then \(\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}}(\widehat V - V)^2} \le |B| + \sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} N^2}\) — a clean root-MSE decomposition.
cards.use: Root-MSE bias–variance splits (sliding-window estimators in non-stationary settings), \(L^p\) error propagation in approximate DP, splitting moment bounds before applying Markov/Chebyshev.

cards.name: Bernoulli's inequality
cards.lay: Raising \((1+x)\) to a power \(n\ge1\) grows at least linearly in \(n\): \((1+x)^n \ge 1+nx\). Useful as a quick lower bound for compound growth or for proving that a geometric quantity is not too small.
cards.st: For \(x \ge -1\) and integer \(n\ge 1\) (or real \(r\ge1\)): \[ (1+x)^r \ge 1 + rx. \] For \(0\le r\le1\) the inequality reverses: \((1+x)^r \le 1+rx\).
ver: Lower bound on \(1-\gamma^H\): \(1-\gamma^H \le H(1-\gamma)\), i.e. \(\gamma^H \ge 1 - H(1-\gamma)\).
Weierstrass product: \(\prod_i(1-x_i) \ge 1 - \sum_i x_i\) for \(x_i\in[0,1]\) (a “union bound for products”).
cards.det:
Proof. Induction for integer \(n\): \((1+x)^{n+1} \ge (1+nx)(1+x) = 1+(n+1)x + nx^2 \ge 1+(n+1)x\). For real \(r\ge1\) it is convexity of \((1+x)^r\) (tangent line at \(x=0\)).

The product version \(\prod(1-x_i)\ge 1-\sum x_i\) is the probabilistic union bound Union bound (Boole's inequality) in disguise: \(\Pr(\text{no bad event}) = \prod(1-p_i)\) for independent events.
cards.ex: The probability that a policy with per-step failure probability \(\delta/H\) survives \(H\) steps is \((1-\delta/H)^H \ge 1-\delta\).
cards.use: Bounding \(1-\gamma^H\), survival probabilities over a horizon, quick lower bounds in lower-bound constructions.

cards.name: Power-mean inequality & \(\ell_p\) norm comparisons
cards.lay: Higher-order means are bigger: the quadratic mean beats the arithmetic mean, which beats the geometric mean. Equivalently, the \(\ell_p\) norms of a vector are ordered, and you can switch between them paying only a dimension factor.
cards.st: For \(x\in{\mathbb{R}}^d\) and \(0<p\le q\le\infty\): \[ {\lVert x\rVert}_q \le {\lVert x\rVert}_p \le d^{\frac1p - \frac1q}{\lVert x\rVert}_q. \] Power means \(M_p(x) = \bigl(\tfrac1d\sum|x_i|^p\bigr)^{1/p}\) are non-decreasing in \(p\).
ver: Most used: \({\lVert x\rVert}_\infty \le {\lVert x\rVert}_2 \le {\lVert x\rVert}_1 \le \sqrt{d}{\lVert x\rVert}_2 \le d{\lVert x\rVert}_\infty\).
QM–AM: \(\tfrac1d\sum x_i \le \sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum x_i^2}\) (Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality).
For random variables: \(p\mapsto ({\mathbb{E}}|X|^p)^{1/p}\) is non-decreasing (Lyapunov's inequality).
cards.det:
Proof idea. \({\lVert x\rVert}_q\le{\lVert x\rVert}_p\): normalise \({\lVert x\rVert}_p=1\), then \(|x_i|\le1\) so \(|x_i|^q\le|x_i|^p\). The other direction is Hölder Hölder's inequality with the all-ones vector.

Lyapunov's inequality for moments follows from Jensen applied to the convex map \(u\mapsto u^{q/p}\).
cards.ex: Converting an \(\ell_2\) concentration bound on \(\widehat P(\cdot|s,a)\) into \(\ell_1\): \({\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_1 \le \sqrt S\,{\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_2\) — the source of the \(\sqrt S\) factor in some tabular bounds.
cards.use: Switching norms between concentration and error-propagation steps; dimension factors in linear function approximation; Lyapunov moment monotonicity in sub-Gaussian characterisations Sub-Gaussian random variables.

cards.name: Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich
cards.lay: The “soft maximum” \(\tfrac1\eta\log\sum_i e^{\eta x_i}\) is within \(\tfrac{\log n}{\eta}\) of the true maximum. This is how entropy regularisation, Hedge, and soft Q-learning approximate a hard max.
cards.st: For \(x\in{\mathbb{R}}^n\) and \(\eta>0\): \[ \max_i x_i \;\le\; \frac{1}{\eta}\log\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\eta x_i} \;\le\; \max_i x_i + \frac{\log n}{\eta}. \]
ver: Variational form: \(\tfrac1\eta\log\sum_i e^{\eta x_i} = \max_{p\in\Delta_n}\bigl\{{\langle p, x\rangle} + \tfrac1\eta H(p)\bigr\}\) with maximiser the softmax \(p_i\propto e^{\eta x_i}\) (see Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle).
Gradient: \(\nabla_x \mathrm{LSE}_\eta(x) = \mathrm{softmax}(\eta x)\); LSE is \(\eta\)-smooth w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\).
Expectation version: \({\mathbb{E}}\max_i X_i \le \tfrac1\eta\log\sum_i{\mathbb{E}} e^{\eta X_i}\) (basis of Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima).
cards.det:
Proof. \(e^{\eta\max x} \le \sum_i e^{\eta x_i} \le n e^{\eta\max x}\); take \(\tfrac1\eta\log\).

The variational form says LSE is the convex conjugate of the negative entropy restricted to the simplex — this is the finite case of the Gibbs variational principle Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle.
cards.ex: Soft value iteration with temperature \(1/\eta\): \(V(s) = \tfrac1\eta\log\sum_a e^{\eta Q(s,a)}\). Per step it overestimates the hard max by at most \(\tfrac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta}\), so the soft optimal value is within \(\tfrac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta(1-\gamma)}\) of \(V^\star\).
cards.use: Entropy-regularised RL (soft Q-learning, SAC theory), Hedge/EXP3 regret, maximal inequalities for sub-Gaussian maxima, smoothing non-smooth max operators in min-max optimisation.

cards.name: Binomial coefficient & Stirling bounds
cards.lay: Practical size estimates for factorials and binomial coefficients. They appear when counting policies, hypotheses, or “which \(k\) out of \(n\)” events in union bounds.
cards.st: For \(1\le k\le n\): \[ \Bigl(\frac{n}{k}\Bigr)^k \le \binom{n}{k} \le \Bigl(\frac{en}{k}\Bigr)^k, \qquad \sqrt{2\pi n}\Bigl(\frac ne\Bigr)^n \le n! \le e\sqrt{n}\Bigl(\frac ne\Bigr)^n. \]
ver: Stirling asymptotics: \(\log n! = n\log n - n + \tfrac12\log(2\pi n) + O(1/n)\).
Entropy bound: \(\binom{n}{k} \le 2^{n h(k/n)}\) where \(h\) is binary entropy; and \(\binom{n}{k} \ge \tfrac{1}{n+1}2^{nh(k/n)}\).
Sum of binomials: \(\sum_{i=0}^k\binom ni \le \bigl(\tfrac{en}{k}\bigr)^k\) (used in Sauer–Shelah VC dimension & Sauer–Shelah lemma).

Number of deterministic policies: \(|{\mathcal{A}}|^{|{\mathcal{S}}|}\), so \(\log(\#\text{policies}) = S\log A\); number of types (empirical distributions) over \(S\) symbols with \(n\) samples \(\le (n+1)^S\).
cards.det: Proof idea. \(\binom nk = \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\tfrac{n-i}{k-i} \ge (n/k)^k\); and \(\binom nk \le \tfrac{n^k}{k!} \le \bigl(\tfrac{en}{k}\bigr)^k\) using \(k! \ge (k/e)^k\) (from \(e^k = \sum k^j/j! \ge k^k/k!\)).
cards.ex: A union bound over all deterministic policies costs \(\log(A^S/\delta) = S\log A + \log(1/\delta)\) inside a Hoeffding bound — giving a \(\sqrt{S\log A}\) dependence; covering arguments Covering & packing numbers (volumetric bound) are used to avoid it when it is too costly.
cards.use: Union bounds over policy classes, the method of types (\(\ell_1\) deviation \(\ell_1\) deviation of the empirical distribution (Weissman et al.)), Sauer–Shelah, lower-bound constructions (Gilbert–Varshamov packings).

cards.name: Inverting \(x \le a + b\sqrt{x}\) and \(x \le a\log x\)
cards.plain: Inverting x ≤ a + b√x and x ≤ a log x
cards.lay: Self-referential bounds — where the quantity you want appears on both sides — are common (regret bounded by \(\sqrt{\text{regret}}\), sample size inside a \(\log\)). These lemmas solve them.
cards.st: Quadratic: if \(x\ge0\) and \(x \le a + b\sqrt{x}\) with \(a,b\ge0\), then \[ x \le \Bigl(\tfrac{b}{2} + \sqrt{\tfrac{b^2}{4}+a}\Bigr)^2 \le 2a + b^2. \] Logarithmic: if \(a\ge1\) and \(x\ge 2a\log(2a)\) then \(x \ge a\log x\). Hence \(x\le a\log x \Rightarrow x \le 2a\log(2a)\).
ver: Sample-size form: \(n \ge \tfrac{c}{{\varepsilon}^2}\log\tfrac{n}{\delta}\) is implied by \(n \ge \tfrac{2c}{{\varepsilon}^2}\log\tfrac{2c}{{\varepsilon}^2\delta}\) (for reasonable constants).
Polynomial form: \(x\le a + bx^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) implies \(x \le \max\{2a, (2b)^{1/(1-\alpha)}\}\).
Lambert-W exact form: the solution of \(x = a\log x\) is \(x = -aW_{-1}(-1/a)\).
cards.det:
Proof (quadratic). Treat \(\sqrt x = y\): \(y^2 - by - a \le 0\) forces \(y \le \tfrac{b+\sqrt{b^2+4a}}{2}\); square and use \((u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2\).

Proof (log). \(g(x)=x - a\log x\) is increasing for \(x>a\); at \(x_0=2a\log(2a)\): \(a\log x_0 = a\log(2a) + a\log\log(2a) \le 2a\log(2a)\) since \(\log\log(2a)\le\log(2a)\).
cards.ex: Variance-aware regret: \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T \le \sqrt{C\,{\mathrm{Reg}}_T\log T} + D\) (e.g. because total variance \(\lesssim\) regret for small-loss bounds) gives \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T \le 2D + C\log T\) — the mechanism behind logarithmic “first-order” bounds.
cards.use: Solving for sample complexity when \(n\) appears inside the confidence log; small-loss / first-order regret bounds; self-bounding arguments with Bernstein/Freedman inequalities.

cards.name: Abel summation (summation by parts)
cards.lay: The discrete analogue of integration by parts: it moves a “difference” from one sequence to the other. Handy when one sequence is monotone (e.g. step sizes, discount weights) and the other has controlled partial sums.
cards.st: With partial sums \(S_k = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\) (\(S_0=0\)): \[ \sum_{k=1}^n a_k b_k = S_n b_n - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S_k\,(b_{k+1}-b_k). \]
ver: Bound form: if \(|S_k|\le M\) for all \(k\) and \(b_k\ge0\) non-increasing, then \(\bigl|\sum_k a_kb_k\bigr| \le M b_1\).
Integral analogue: \(\int_a^b f g' = [fg]_a^b - \int_a^b f' g\).
cards.det: Abel summation is the tool for weighted sums of martingale differences with deterministic decreasing weights (as in stochastic approximation with step sizes \(\alpha_t\)): it reduces the weighted sum to unweighted partial sums, which are controlled by Azuma Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales) or a maximal inequality Doob's maximal inequalities.
cards.ex: If \(|\sum_{k\le n}\xi_k| \le C\sqrt{n\log n}\) for all \(n\) and \(\alpha_k = 1/k\), then \(|\sum_{k\le n}\alpha_k\xi_k| \le \tfrac{C\sqrt{n\log n}}{n} + \sum_k C\sqrt{k\log k}\bigl(\tfrac1k - \tfrac{1}{k+1}\bigr) = O(1)\) up to logs, showing almost-sure convergence of weighted noise sums.
cards.use: Stochastic approximation with decaying steps, discounted/weighted estimators in non-stationary bandits, converting uniform partial-sum bounds into bounds for weighted sums.

cards.name: Rearrangement & Chebyshev's sum inequality
cards.lay: Pairing large with large gives the biggest sum of products; pairing large with small the smallest. Chebyshev's sum inequality is the averaged version: similarly ordered sequences are positively correlated.
cards.st: If \(a_1\le\dots\le a_n\) and \(b_1\le\dots\le b_n\), then for any permutation \(\sigma\) \[ \sum_i a_i b_{n+1-i} \le \sum_i a_ib_{\sigma(i)} \le \sum_i a_ib_i, \qquad \frac1n\sum_i a_ib_i \ge \Bigl(\frac1n\sum_i a_i\Bigr)\Bigl(\frac1n\sum_i b_i\Bigr). \]
ver: Probabilistic (Chebyshev association / Harris): if \(f,g\) are both non-decreasing, \({\mathbb{E}}[f(X)g(X)] \ge {\mathbb{E}} f(X)\,{\mathbb{E}} g(X)\).
cards.det: Proof by exchange: if \(i<j\) but \(b_{\sigma(i)} > b_{\sigma(j)}\), swapping increases the sum by \((a_j-a_i)(b_{\sigma(i)}-b_{\sigma(j)})\ge0\). Chebyshev's sum inequality follows from \(\sum_{i,j}(a_i-a_j)(b_i-b_j)\ge0\).
cards.ex: In monotone MDPs (values non-decreasing in state, transitions stochastically monotone), association inequalities show that \({\mathbb{E}}[V(s')R(s')]\ge{\mathbb{E}} V(s'){\mathbb{E}} R(s')\), used in structured-policy proofs.
cards.use: Occasional: structural results for monotone policies, proving optimality of index orderings, correlation inequalities in lower-bound constructions.

cards.name: Dual norms & norm equivalence
cards.lay: Every norm has a “partner” (its dual) that measures how large an inner product can be. In finite dimensions all norms are equivalent up to constants, so you can switch norms at a dimension-dependent price.
cards.st: The dual norm of \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) is \({\lVert y\rVert}_* = \sup_{{\lVert x\rVert}\le1}{\langle x, y\rangle}\), and \({\langle x, y\rangle} \le {\lVert x\rVert}\,{\lVert y\rVert}_*\) (generalised Cauchy–Schwarz). The dual of \(\ell_p\) is \(\ell_q\) with \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1\). In \({\mathbb{R}}^d\), for any two norms there are \(c,C>0\) with \(c{\lVert x\rVert}_a\le{\lVert x\rVert}_b\le C{\lVert x\rVert}_a\).
ver: Dual pairs: \((\ell_1,\ell_\infty)\), \((\ell_2,\ell_2)\), \(({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_A, {\lVert \cdot\rVert}_{A^{-1}})\) for \(A\succ0\), (operator norm, nuclear norm).
Bidual: \({\lVert x\rVert}_{**} = {\lVert x\rVert}\) (finite dimensions).
Explicit constants: see Power-mean inequality & \(\ell_p\) norm comparisons for \(\ell_p\) comparisons.
cards.det: Dual norms are the language of mirror descent and of first-order optimality: gradients live in the dual space, so step sizes and Lipschitz constants are measured in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_*\). For entropic mirror descent on the simplex, the primal norm is \(\ell_1\) and gradients are measured in \(\ell_\infty\) — which is why Hedge regret depends on \(\max_i|\ell_{t,i}|\) rather than \({\lVert \ell_t\rVert}_2\).
cards.ex: \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_A\) with \(A = \lambda I + \sum_s x_sx_s^\top\) has dual \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_{A^{-1}}\); the linear-bandit confidence width is \({\lVert x\rVert}_{A^{-1}}\cdot{\lVert \hat\theta-\theta\rVert}_A\).
cards.use: Mirror descent geometry; Lipschitz constants for policy optimisation; confidence ellipsoids; converting concentration in one norm into errors in another.

cards.name: Induced operator norms (\(\ell_\infty\) norm of stochastic matrices)
cards.plain: Induced operator norms (ℓ_∞ norm of stochastic matrices)
cards.lay: The operator norm says how much a matrix can stretch a vector. For the max-norm it equals the largest absolute row sum — so a transition matrix (rows sum to one) never increases the sup-norm of a value function.
cards.st: For \(A\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times n}\), \({\lVert A\rVert}_{p\to p} = \sup_{x\ne0}\tfrac{{\lVert Ax\rVert}_p}{{\lVert x\rVert}_p}\) and \[ {\lVert A\rVert}_{\infty\to\infty} = \max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|, \quad {\lVert A\rVert}_{1\to1} = \max_j\sum_i|A_{ij}|, \quad {\lVert A\rVert}_{2\to2} = \sigma_{\max}(A). \] In particular, for a row-stochastic \(P\): \({\lVert PV\rVert}_\infty \le {\lVert V\rVert}_\infty\).
ver: Sub-multiplicativity: \({\lVert AB\rVert}\le{\lVert A\rVert}{\lVert B\rVert}\) and \({\lVert Ax\rVert}\le{\lVert A\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}\).

Stochastic matrices also preserve the span: \({\operatorname{sp}}(PV)\le{\operatorname{sp}}(V)\); and with Dobrushin coefficient \(\delta(P) = \tfrac12\max_{i,j}{\lVert P_{i\cdot}-P_{j\cdot}\rVert}_1\), \({\operatorname{sp}}(PV)\le\delta(P){\operatorname{sp}}(V)\) Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.

Left action on distributions: \({\lVert \mu^\top P\rVert}_1 \le {\lVert \mu\rVert}_1\) and \({\lVert (\mu-\nu)^\top P\rVert}_1 \le {\lVert \mu-\nu\rVert}_1\) (data processing for TV Data-processing inequality).
Spectral radius: \(\rho(A) \le {\lVert A\rVert}\) for any induced norm; \(\rho(A) = \lim_k{\lVert A^k\rVert}^{1/k}\) (Gelfand).
cards.det: Because \((PV)(s) = \sum_{s'}P(s'|s)V(s')\) is an average of entries of \(V\), \(|(PV)(s)|\le\max_{s'}|V(s')|\). This one-line fact is the reason the Bellman operator \(T^\pi V = r + \gamma P^\pi V\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in sup-norm Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators.
cards.ex: \({\lVert T^\pi V - T^\pi U\rVert}_\infty = \gamma{\lVert P^\pi(V-U)\rVert}_\infty \le \gamma{\lVert V-U\rVert}_\infty\).
cards.use: Contraction of Bellman operators, bounding \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\), error propagation, mixing analysis via Dobrushin coefficients.

cards.name: Spectral theorem for symmetric matrices
cards.lay: A symmetric matrix is just a scaling along some orthogonal set of directions. Everything about it (norms, inverses, square roots, \(\log\det\)) can be computed from its eigenvalues.
cards.st: If \(A\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d}\) is symmetric, there is an orthogonal \(U\) and real diagonal \(\Lambda\) with \[ A = U\Lambda U^\top = \sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i u_iu_i^\top. \]
ver: Functional calculus: \(f(A) = Uf(\Lambda)U^\top\) (e.g. \(A^{1/2}\), \(A^{-1}\), \(\log A\), \(e^A\)).
\({\operatorname{tr}} A = \sum\lambda_i\), \(\det A = \prod\lambda_i\), \({\lVert A\rVert}_2 = \max|\lambda_i|\), \({\lVert A\rVert}_F^2=\sum\lambda_i^2\).
Normal matrices (complex): unitary diagonalisation. Non-symmetric matrices (e.g. transition matrices) need Jordan or Schur forms instead.
Self-adjoint compact operators on Hilbert spaces (infinite-dimensional version).
cards.det: In RL, the matrices that are symmetric are typically design/Gram matrices \(\Sigma=\sum\phi\phi^\top\), Fisher information matrices (natural policy gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence), and Hessians. Transition matrices are generally not symmetric — but reversible chains are symmetric in \(L^2(\pi)\), which gives clean spectral-gap mixing bounds Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.
cards.ex: For \(V = \lambda I + \sum_{s<t}x_sx_s^\top\), \(\log\det V = \sum_i\log\lambda_i(V)\) and AM–GM on eigenvalues gives \(\log\det V \le d\log({\operatorname{tr}} V/d) \le d\log(\lambda + tL^2/d)\) — the bound inside Elliptical potential lemma.
cards.use: LinUCB/OFUL analysis, natural gradient (Fisher matrix), LSTD stability (eigenvalues of \(\Phi^\top D(I-\gamma P)\Phi\)), spectral-gap mixing.

cards.name: Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\)
cards.lay: If a matrix \(A\) is “small” (norm below 1), then \(I-A\) is invertible and its inverse is \(I + A + A^2 + \dots\) — a matrix geometric series. In RL this is the formula \(V^\pi = (I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}r^\pi\).
cards.st: If \({\lVert A\rVert}<1\) in some sub-multiplicative norm, then \(I-A\) is invertible, \[ (I-A)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty A^k, \qquad {\lVert (I-A)^{-1}\rVert} \le \frac{1}{1-{\lVert A\rVert}}. \] For a stochastic \(P\) and \(\gamma<1\): \(V^\pi = (I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}r^\pi\), and \((1-\gamma)(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) is itself a stochastic matrix.
ver: Condition is really on the spectral radius: the series converges iff \(\rho(A)<1\).
Perturbed inverse: \((I-A-E)^{-1} - (I-A)^{-1} = (I-A-E)^{-1}E(I-A)^{-1}\) (resolvent identity; see Perturbation of inverses (Banach lemma)).
Entrywise: \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\ge0\) entrywise and has row sums \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) — it is monotone: \(r\le r'\Rightarrow V\le V'\).
Rows define the discounted occupancy: \(d_s^\pi = (1-\gamma)e_s^\top(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) Discounted occupancy measures.
cards.det:
This identity is the algebraic heart of discounted MDPs. Its probabilistic meaning: \([(I-\gamma P)^{-1}]_{s,s'} = \sum_t\gamma^t\Pr(s_t=s'\mid s_0=s)\), the expected discounted number of visits.

Comparing two resolvents gives the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error): \(V^\pi_{\widehat M} - V^\pi_M = \gamma(I-\gamma\widehat P^\pi)^{-1}(\widehat P^\pi - P^\pi)V^\pi_M\).
cards.ex: Policy evaluation by solving a linear system: \(V^\pi = (I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}r^\pi\), with \({\lVert V^\pi\rVert}_\infty \le \tfrac{{\lVert r\rVert}_\infty}{1-\gamma}\) — exactly the Neumann bound.
cards.use: Policy evaluation, simulation lemma, occupancy measures, LSTD, sensitivity of values to perturbations of \(P\) (non-stationary drift), Laurent expansions for average reward Poisson equation, bias & Laurent expansion (average reward).

cards.name: Rayleigh quotient & Courant–Fischer min–max
cards.lay: The largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix is the maximum of \(x^\top Ax\) over unit vectors; the other eigenvalues are characterised by min–max games over subspaces. Great for bounding eigenvalues without computing them.
cards.st: For symmetric \(A\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_d\): \[ \lambda_1 = \max_{{\lVert x\rVert}=1}x^\top Ax,\qquad \lambda_d = \min_{{\lVert x\rVert}=1}x^\top Ax,\qquad \lambda_k = \max_{\dim S=k}\;\min_{x\in S,{\lVert x\rVert}=1}x^\top Ax. \]
ver: Generalised Rayleigh quotient: \(\max_x\tfrac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top Bx} = \lambda_{\max}(B^{-1/2}AB^{-1/2})\) for \(B\succ0\).
Consequence: \(\lambda_{\min}(A){\lVert x\rVert}^2 \le x^\top Ax \le \lambda_{\max}(A){\lVert x\rVert}^2\).
Cauchy interlacing: eigenvalues of a principal submatrix interlace those of \(A\).
cards.det: Courant–Fischer is the engine behind Weyl's inequality Weyl's inequality (eigenvalue perturbation) and many “minimum eigenvalue” assumptions: e.g. coverage assumptions in offline RL require \(\lambda_{\min}({\mathbb{E}}_\mu[\phi\phi^\top])\ge\kappa\), meaning \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu(\phi^\top v)^2 \ge\kappa{\lVert v\rVert}^2\) for every direction \(v\).
cards.ex: With \(\Sigma = {\mathbb{E}}_\mu[\phi\phi^\top]\succeq\kappa I\), the relative condition number between target and data distributions is \(\max_v\tfrac{v^\top\Sigma_{\pi}v}{v^\top\Sigma v}\) — a generalised Rayleigh quotient that appears in offline linear RL bounds.
cards.use: Coverage/conditioning assumptions, relative condition numbers in policy-gradient theory (NPG with function approximation), PCA-type feature arguments.

cards.name: Weyl's inequality (eigenvalue perturbation)
cards.lay: Adding a small symmetric perturbation can only move each eigenvalue by at most the size of the perturbation. Eigenvalues are 1-Lipschitz functions of the matrix in operator norm.
cards.st: For symmetric \(A,E\) with ordered eigenvalues, \[ |\lambda_i(A+E) - \lambda_i(A)| \le {\lVert E\rVert}_2 \quad\text{for every } i. \]
ver: Sharper: \(\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_d(E) \le \lambda_i(A+E) \le \lambda_i(A)+\lambda_1(E)\).
Singular values: \(|\sigma_i(A+E)-\sigma_i(A)| \le {\lVert E\rVert}_2\) for any (non-symmetric) matrices.
Hoffman–Wielandt: \(\sum_i(\lambda_i(A+E)-\lambda_i(A))^2 \le {\lVert E\rVert}_F^2\) (symmetric case).
cards.det: Follows directly from Courant–Fischer Rayleigh quotient & Courant–Fischer min–max. Combined with matrix concentration (e.g. matrix Bernstein Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp)) it shows that the empirical covariance \(\widehat\Sigma\) inherits a lower eigenvalue bound from \(\Sigma\): \(\lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Sigma)\ge\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma) - {\lVert \widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\rVert}_2\).
cards.ex: If \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)=\kappa\) and \(n \gtrsim \tfrac{L^2\log(d/\delta)}{\kappa^2}\) samples with \({\lVert \phi\rVert}\le L\), then w.h.p. \(\lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Sigma)\ge\kappa/2\).
cards.use: Offline RL with linear features, LSTD/FQI conditioning, spectral methods for latent-variable models (method of moments alternatives to EM).

cards.name: Singular value decomposition & Eckart–Young
cards.lay: Every matrix is a rotation, then an axis-aligned scaling, then another rotation. Truncating the SVD gives the best low-rank approximation — the backbone of low-rank MDP and representation-learning theory.
cards.st: Any \(A\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times n}\) factors as \(A = U\Sigma V^\top=\sum_i\sigma_iu_iv_i^\top\) with orthonormal \(U,V\) and \(\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\dots\ge0\). (Eckart–Young–Mirsky) For every \(k\), \[ \min_{\mathrm{rank}(B)\le k}{\lVert A-B\rVert} = {\lVert A - A_k\rVert}, \quad A_k=\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^\top, \] for both the spectral norm (\(=\sigma_{k+1}\)) and Frobenius norm (\(=\sqrt{\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}\)).
ver: Pseudo-inverse: \(A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^\top\); least squares solution \(\hat\theta = \Phi^+ y\).
Nuclear norm \({\lVert A\rVert}_* = \sum\sigma_i\) is dual to the spectral norm.
Polar decomposition \(A = QS\) with \(Q\) orthogonal, \(S\succeq0\).
cards.det: Low-rank MDPs assume \(P(s'|s,a) = {\langle \phi(s,a), \mu(s')\rangle}\) with \(d\)-dimensional factors — a rank-\(d\) factorisation of the transition matrix. Eckart–Young tells you what is lost when you truncate to rank \(k<d\).
cards.ex: Representation learning in a rank-\(d\) MDP: the best rank-\(k\) approximation of the \(SA\times S\) transition matrix incurs error \(\sigma_{k+1}\) in operator norm, which propagates to values via the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error).
cards.use: Low-rank MDPs, linear MDP feature design, matrix completion views of Q-learning, PCA of state representations.

cards.name: Sherman–Morrison & Woodbury identities
cards.lay: How the inverse of a matrix changes after a rank-one (or low-rank) update. It gives cheap recursive least squares and is central to analysing how confidence ellipsoids shrink as data arrives.
cards.st: For invertible \(A\) and vectors \(u,v\) with \(1+v^\top A^{-1}u\ne0\): \[ (A+uv^\top)^{-1} = A^{-1} - \frac{A^{-1}uv^\top A^{-1}}{1+v^\top A^{-1}u}. \] Woodbury: \((A+UCV)^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U)^{-1}VA^{-1}\).
ver: Symmetric rank-one update: \((V+xx^\top)^{-1} = V^{-1} - \tfrac{V^{-1}xx^\top V^{-1}}{1+{\lVert x\rVert}_{V^{-1}}^2}\).
Consequence: \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{(V+xx^\top)^{-1}} = \tfrac{{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}}{1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}} < 1\).
Push-through identity: \((I+AB)^{-1}A = A(I+BA)^{-1}\).
cards.det: Proof: multiply the right-hand side by \(A+uv^\top\) and simplify. Woodbury is the same computation in block form. Recursive least squares (used inside LinUCB, LSTD with online updates, Kalman filtering) is nothing but Sherman–Morrison applied each round, costing \(O(d^2)\) instead of \(O(d^3)\).
cards.ex: In OFUL/LinUCB, after playing \(x_t\) the design matrix becomes \(V_t = V_{t-1}+x_tx_t^\top\); Sherman–Morrison gives the new inverse in \(O(d^2)\) and shows the uncertainty in direction \(x_t\) shrinks by factor \(1/(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\).
cards.use: Recursive least squares in linear bandits/LSTD, Gaussian-process posterior updates, Kalman filters for non-stationary tracking, proving the matrix determinant lemma.

cards.name: Matrix determinant lemma
cards.lay: The determinant after a rank-one update is the old determinant times a simple scalar factor. Taking logs, the “information gained” by adding \(x\) is \(\log(1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}})\), which telescopes over time.
cards.st: For invertible \(A\) and vectors \(u,v\): \[ \det(A+uv^\top) = (1+v^\top A^{-1}u)\det A. \] In particular \(\log\det(V+xx^\top) = \log\det V + \log(1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}})\).
ver: Low rank: \(\det(A+UWV^\top) = \det(W^{-1}+V^\top A^{-1}U)\det W\det A\).
Sylvester: \(\det(I_m + AB) = \det(I_n+BA)\).
Determinant–trace bound: \(\det V \le ({\operatorname{tr}} V/d)^d\) (AM–GM on eigenvalues AM–GM inequality).
cards.det: Telescoping the log-det identity over \(t\) gives \(\sum_t\log(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}) = \log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\) — the main step of the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma. The right-hand side is \(O(d\log T)\) by the determinant–trace bound.
cards.ex: With \(V_0=\lambda I\), \({\lVert x_t\rVert}\le L\): \(\log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0} \le d\log\bigl(1+\tfrac{TL^2}{d\lambda}\bigr)\).
cards.use: Elliptical potential lemma; information-gain bounds in GP-UCB; self-normalised confidence radius Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.); linear MDP regret.

cards.name: Loewner order facts
cards.lay: \(A\succeq B\) means \(A-B\) is positive semidefinite: “\(A\) is bigger in every direction”. Several familiar scalar facts carry over (inverse reverses order, square root preserves it) but some do not (squaring does not).
cards.st: For symmetric \(A,B\) with \(A\succeq B\succ0\): \[ B^{-1}\succeq A^{-1},\quad A^{1/2}\succeq B^{1/2},\quad {\operatorname{tr}} A\ge{\operatorname{tr}} B,\quad \det A\ge\det B,\quad {\lVert x\rVert}_{A^{-1}}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_{B^{-1}}. \]
ver: Congruence: \(A\succeq B\Rightarrow C^\top AC\succeq C^\top BC\).
Operator monotone functions: \(\log\) and \(t\mapsto t^p\) for \(p\in[0,1]\) preserve order; \(t^2\) does not.
Ratio bound: if \(A\succeq B\succ0\) then \(\sup_x\tfrac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top Bx} \le \tfrac{\det A}{\det B}\) (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., used in rarely-switching bandits).
cards.det: The determinant-ratio bound is what justifies “rarely switching” and batched linear bandits: you only recompute the policy when \(\det V_t\) has doubled, and in between the confidence ellipsoid changes by at most a constant factor. The number of switches is \(O(d\log T)\).
cards.ex: Because \(V_t\succeq V_{t-1}\), uncertainty \({\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\) is non-increasing in \(t\) for every fixed \(x\) — confidence widths never grow when you add data (with ridge regularisation).
cards.use: Monotonicity of confidence widths, rarely-switching algorithms (low policy-switching cost), batch RL, comparing Fisher information matrices.

cards.name: Perron–Frobenius theorem
cards.lay: A non-negative matrix that connects everything (irreducible) has a unique largest positive eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. For a transition matrix that eigenvalue is 1 and the (left) eigenvector is the stationary distribution.
cards.st: Let \(A\ge0\) entrywise be irreducible. Then the spectral radius \(\rho(A)>0\) is a simple eigenvalue with left and right eigenvectors that are entrywise strictly positive, and every other eigenvalue satisfies \(|\lambda|\le\rho(A)\). If \(A\) is also aperiodic (primitive), \(|\lambda|<\rho(A)\) for all other eigenvalues.
ver: Stochastic matrices: \(\rho(P)=1\), right eigenvector \({\mathbf{1}}\), left eigenvector the stationary distribution \(\mu\) (\(\mu^\top P=\mu^\top\)) Existence & uniqueness of stationary distributions.
Positive matrices (Perron's original theorem): strict positivity gives a spectral gap automatically.
Collatz–Wielandt formula: \(\rho(A) = \max_{x\ge0,x\ne0}\min_{i:x_i>0}\tfrac{(Ax)_i}{x_i}\).
cards.det: The gap between \(1\) and the second-largest eigenvalue modulus governs how fast \(P^t\) converges to \({\mathbf{1}}\mu^\top\) Mixing time & geometric ergodicity. In average-reward RL, unichain/ergodicity assumptions are Perron–Frobenius conditions that make the gain independent of the start state.
cards.ex: For the two-state chain with flip probabilities \(p\) and \(q\), eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(1-p-q\); the stationary distribution is \(\bigl(\tfrac{q}{p+q},\tfrac{p}{p+q}\bigr)\) and \({\lVert P^t(x,\cdot)-\mu\rVert}_{{\mathrm{TV}}}\propto|1-p-q|^t\).
cards.use: Existence/uniqueness of stationary distributions, average-reward MDPs, PageRank-type arguments, mixing-time analyses for policy evaluation from single trajectories.

cards.name: Perturbation of inverses (Banach lemma)
cards.lay: If \(A\) is invertible and \(E\) is small relative to \(A^{-1}\), then \(A+E\) is still invertible and its inverse is close to \(A^{-1}\). Quantifies how sensitive value functions are to model errors.
cards.st: If \({\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}<1\) then \(A+E\) is invertible and \[ {\lVert (A+E)^{-1}\rVert}\le\frac{{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}}{1-{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}},\qquad {\lVert (A+E)^{-1}-A^{-1}\rVert}\le\frac{{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}^2{\lVert E\rVert}}{1-{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}}. \]
ver: Resolvent identity: \(B^{-1}-A^{-1} = B^{-1}(A-B)A^{-1}\) (exact, no smallness needed).
Condition-number form: \(\tfrac{{\lVert \delta x\rVert}}{{\lVert x\rVert}}\le\kappa(A)\tfrac{{\lVert \delta b\rVert}}{{\lVert b\rVert}}\) for \(Ax=b\).
cards.det: Apply with \(A = I-\gamma P\), \(E = -\gamma(\widehat P - P)\): since \({\lVert (I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) for any stochastic \(\widehat P\), the resolvent identity directly gives the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error) without any smallness condition.
cards.ex: \(V_{\widehat P} - V_P = [(I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}-(I-\gamma P)^{-1}]r = \gamma(I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}(\widehat P-P)(I-\gamma P)^{-1}r\), so \({\lVert V_{\widehat P}-V_P\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\gamma{\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_{\infty\to\infty}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\).
cards.use: Sensitivity of values to model error (model-based RL, non-stationary drift), LSTD perturbation analysis, robustness of linear system solutions.

cards.name: Schur complement & block inversion
cards.lay: For a \(2\times2\) block matrix, the Schur complement is “what is left” after eliminating one block. It tells you when a block matrix is positive definite and gives formulas for conditional Gaussians.
cards.st: For \(M = \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^\top&C\end{pmatrix}\) with \(A\succ0\): \(M\succeq0 \iff C - B^\top A^{-1}B\succeq0\), and \[ \det M = \det A\,\det(C-B^\top A^{-1}B). \]
ver: Block inverse: the lower-right block of \(M^{-1}\) equals \((C-B^\top A^{-1}B)^{-1}\).
Gaussian conditioning: if \((X,Y)\) is jointly Gaussian then \({\operatorname{Cov}}(Y\mid X) = \Sigma_{YY}-\Sigma_{YX}\Sigma_{XX}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}\) — a Schur complement.
Used to prove \(\begin{pmatrix}A & x\\ x^\top & t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0 \iff t\ge x^\top A^{-1}x\) (SDP representation of \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{A^{-1}}\)).
cards.det: Schur complements show up in EM theory as the missing-information matrix: observed Fisher information \(=\) complete information \(-\) missing information Missing-information principle (Louis) & EM's convergence rate, a Schur-complement-like subtraction.
cards.ex: Kalman filter update: posterior covariance \(= \Sigma - \Sigma H^\top(H\Sigma H^\top + R)^{-1}H\Sigma\), a Schur complement — used in tracking drifting parameters in non-stationary bandits.
cards.use: Gaussian posterior computations (Thompson sampling with linear-Gaussian models), SDP relaxations, missing information in EM, block-structured LSTD.

cards.name: Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality
cards.plain: Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality
cards.lay: The trace of a product is bounded by pairing singular values: largest with largest. Most often used as \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\le{\lVert A\rVert}_2{\operatorname{tr}}(B)\) for positive semidefinite \(B\).
cards.st: (von Neumann) For \(A,B\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times n}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1\ge\dots\) and \(\tau_1\ge\dots\): \[ |{\operatorname{tr}}(AB)| \le \sum_i\sigma_i(A)\tau_i(B). \] Consequently \(|{\operatorname{tr}}(AB)|\le{\lVert A\rVert}_2{\lVert B\rVert}_*\) and, for \(B\succeq0\), \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\le\lambda_{\max}(A){\operatorname{tr}} B\).
ver: Cauchy–Schwarz for matrices: \(|{\operatorname{tr}}(A^\top B)|\le{\lVert A\rVert}_F{\lVert B\rVert}_F\).
Golden–Thompson: \({\operatorname{tr}} e^{A+B}\le{\operatorname{tr}}(e^Ae^B)\) for symmetric \(A,B\) (used to prove matrix Chernoff bounds Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp)).
Lieb's concavity theorem (deep; drives Tropp's matrix concentration).
cards.det: The workhorse corollary: \({\mathbb{E}}[x^\top Ax] = {\operatorname{tr}}(A\,{\mathbb{E}}[xx^\top]) \le \lambda_{\max}(A)\,{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert x\rVert}^2\). Expressions like \({\mathbb{E}}_{\phi\sim d^\pi}{\lVert \phi\rVert}^2_{\Sigma^{-1}} = {\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi)\) (relative coverage) are traces of products.
cards.ex: If the data covariance is \(\Sigma\) and the target-policy covariance is \(\Sigma_\pi\), the offline error is often proportional to \(\sqrt{{\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi)}\le\sqrt{d\,\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{-1/2}\Sigma_\pi\Sigma^{-1/2})}\).
cards.use: Coverage coefficients in offline linear RL, expected squared feature norms, matrix concentration proofs.

cards.name: Gershgorin circle theorem
cards.lay: Every eigenvalue of a matrix lies close to some diagonal entry — within a disc whose radius is the sum of the off-diagonal magnitudes in that row. A quick way to prove a matrix is non-singular or stable.
cards.st: Every eigenvalue of \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) lies in \(\bigcup_i D_i\), where \[ D_i = \Bigl\{z: |z-A_{ii}|\le\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\Bigr\}. \]
ver: Column version (apply to \(A^\top\)).
Strict diagonal dominance \(\Rightarrow\) invertibility (Levy–Desplanques).
cards.det: Useful in stochastic approximation: the ODE \(\dot\theta = A\theta + b\) is stable iff \(A\) is Hurwitz. For tabular TD(0), \(A = D(\gamma P - I)\) where \(D\) is the diagonal of the stationary distribution — Gershgorin-type diagonal dominance arguments (together with the \(\mu\)-weighted norm) show its eigenvalues have negative real parts.
cards.ex: Matrix \(I-\gamma P\) with stochastic \(P\): diagonal entries \(1-\gamma P_{ii}\), off-diagonal row sum \(\gamma(1-P_{ii})\); every disc lies in \(\{\mathrm{Re}\,z\ge1-\gamma\}\), so \(I-\gamma P\) is invertible (consistent with Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\)).
cards.use: Stability of linear stochastic approximation (TD, GTD), quick invertibility checks, bounding spectra of iteration matrices.

cards.name: Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping)
cards.lay: If applying a map always brings any two points closer together by a fixed factor \(\gamma<1\), then repeatedly applying it from anywhere converges — fast — to a unique point that the map leaves unchanged. This is why value iteration works.
cards.st: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space and \(T:X\to X\) satisfy \(d(Tx,Ty)\le\gamma\,d(x,y)\) for some \(\gamma\in[0,1)\). Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^\star\), and for any \(x_0\), \(x_k=T^kx_0\) satisfies \[ d(x_k,x^\star)\le\gamma^kd(x_0,x^\star)\le\frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma}d(x_0,x_1). \]
ver: A posteriori bound: \(d(x_k,x^\star)\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d(x_k,x_{k+1})\) — gives a computable stopping rule for value iteration.
Eventually contractive maps: if \(T^m\) is a contraction for some \(m\), \(T\) still has a unique fixed point (useful for undiscounted SSPs with proper policies).
Weighted sup-norm contractions: for stochastic shortest path problems, \(T\) is a contraction in \({\lVert V\rVert}_{\infty,w}=\max_s|V(s)|/w(s)\) for a suitable \(w>0\).
Inexact iteration: if \({\lVert x_{k+1}-Tx_k\rVert}\le{\varepsilon}\) then \(\limsup_k d(x_k,x^\star)\le\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\) Geometric series & discounted sums.
Non-expansive maps (\(\gamma=1\)) need not have unique fixed points; see Brouwer/Kakutani Brouwer & Kakutani fixed-point theorems for existence without contraction.
cards.det:
Proof. \(d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le\gamma^kd(x_1,x_0)\), so \((x_k)\) is Cauchy by the geometric series Geometric series & discounted sums; completeness gives a limit, continuity of \(T\) makes it a fixed point; two fixed points \(x,y\) would satisfy \(d(x,y)\le\gamma d(x,y)\), forcing \(x=y\).

In RL the space is \(({\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{S}}},{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty)\) (complete), and the maps are \(T^\pi\), \(T^\star\) Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators. Population EM is a contraction near \(\theta^\star\) under the Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu conditions Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction, which is how local linear convergence of EM is proved.
cards.ex: Value iteration: \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma^k{\lVert V_0-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma}\) for rewards in \([0,1]\), \(V_0=0\). To reach accuracy \({\varepsilon}\) you need \(k\ge\tfrac{\log(1/({\varepsilon}(1-\gamma)))}{1-\gamma}\) iterations.
cards.use: Existence/uniqueness of \(V^\pi\), \(V^\star\), \(Q^\star\); value iteration rates; fitted value iteration error propagation; local convergence of EM and other fixed-point algorithms; existence of solutions to Bellman equations in robust and regularised MDPs.

cards.name: Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\)
cards.lay: The maximum of a function changes by at most the largest pointwise change of the function. This tiny fact is what makes the Bellman optimality operator a contraction, despite the nonlinear max.
cards.st: For bounded functions \(f,g\) on any set \({\mathcal{A}}\): \[ \Bigl|\sup_{a}f(a)-\sup_{a}g(a)\Bigr|\le\sup_a|f(a)-g(a)|. \] The same holds with \(\inf\), and for \(\max\) over finite sets.
ver: Soft-max version: \(|\mathrm{LSE}_\eta(x)-\mathrm{LSE}_\eta(y)|\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}_\infty\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
Min–max: \(|\max_a\min_b f - \max_a\min_b g|\le{\lVert f-g\rVert}_\infty\) (Shapley/Markov games operator is a contraction).
Expectation of max: \(|{\mathbb{E}}\max_a X_a - {\mathbb{E}}\max_a Y_a|\le{\mathbb{E}}\max_a|X_a-Y_a|\).
cards.det:
Proof. For any \(a\), \(f(a)\le g(a)+\sup|f-g|\le\sup g+\sup|f-g|\); take sup over \(a\), then swap roles of \(f\) and \(g\).

Consequence: \(|(T^\star V)(s)-(T^\star U)(s)| = \gamma|\max_a P_{s,a}^\top V - \max_a P_{s,a}^\top U|\le\gamma\max_a|P_{s,a}^\top(V-U)|\le\gamma{\lVert V-U\rVert}_\infty\).
cards.ex: Zero-sum Markov games: the Shapley operator \((TV)(s) = \max_{x}\min_{y}x^\top[r(s)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s')V(s')]y\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction by the min–max version.
cards.use: Contraction of \(T^\star\); Lipschitzness of \(V^\star\) in rewards/transitions (non-stationary drift analyses); stability of greedy policies; Markov games.

cards.name: Mean value theorem
cards.lay: Over any interval, a smooth function's average slope equals its actual slope at some point in between. So bounds on derivatives turn directly into Lipschitz bounds.
cards.st: If \(f:[a,b]\to{\mathbb{R}}\) is continuous and differentiable on \((a,b)\), there is \(c\in(a,b)\) with \(f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)\). For \(f:{\mathbb{R}}^d\to{\mathbb{R}}\): \(f(y)-f(x)={\langle \nabla f(z), y-x\rangle}\) for some \(z\) on the segment \([x,y]\).
ver: Lipschitz consequence: \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le\sup_z{\lVert \nabla f(z)\rVert}_*{\lVert y-x\rVert}\).

Vector-valued maps: no exact MVT, but the integral form \(F(y)-F(x)=\int_0^1J_F(x+t(y-x))(y-x)\,{\mathrm{d}} t\) gives \({\lVert F(y)-F(x)\rVert}\le\sup{\lVert J_F\rVert}{\lVert y-x\rVert}\) Taylor's theorem with remainder.
Cauchy's MVT: \((f(b)-f(a))g'(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(c)\) (behind L'Hôpital).
cards.det: Typical RL usage: bounding the change in a policy's value as parameters move, by bounding the gradient norm (policy-gradient Lipschitz constants), or showing the EM map is a contraction via \(\sup{\lVert \nabla M(\theta)\rVert}_2<1\) Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction.
cards.ex: For softmax policies, \({\lVert \nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}\rVert}_2\le\tfrac{\sqrt2}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) (rewards in \([0,1]\)), so \(|V^{\pi_\theta}-V^{\pi_{\theta'}}|\le\tfrac{\sqrt2}{(1-\gamma)^2}{\lVert \theta-\theta'\rVert}_2\).
cards.use: Lipschitz bounds for value functions in parameters; contraction proofs via Jacobian bounds; linearisation arguments.

cards.name: Taylor's theorem with remainder
cards.lay: Near any point, a smooth function is approximately its tangent line (or tangent parabola), and the error is controlled by the next derivative. Every “smooth implies descent” and “local quadratic” argument is Taylor.
cards.st: If \(f\in C^{k+1}\) near \(x\): \[ f(x+h)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{f^{(j)}(x)}{j!}h^j+R_k,\quad R_k=\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi)}{(k+1)!}h^{k+1}=\int_0^1\frac{(1-t)^k}{k!}f^{(k+1)}(x+th)h^{k+1}{\mathrm{d}} t. \] Multivariate second order: \(f(x+h)=f(x)+{\langle \nabla f(x), h\rangle}+\tfrac12h^\top\nabla^2f(\xi)h\).
ver: Integral (first-order) form: \(f(y)=f(x)+\int_0^1{\langle \nabla f(x+t(y-x)), y-x\rangle}{\mathrm{d}} t\).
Gradient-Lipschitz consequence: \(|f(y)-f(x)-{\langle \nabla f(x), y-x\rangle}|\le\tfrac L2{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\) \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma.
Peano remainder: \(R_k=o(h^k)\) as \(h\to0\) (no explicit constant).

Taylor for log-MGF: \(\log{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X}=\lambda{\mathbb{E}} X+\tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}{\operatorname{Var}} X+O(\lambda^3)\) — motivates sub-Gaussian definitions Sub-Gaussian random variables.
cards.det: Taylor expansions underpin: the descent lemma \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma; Hoeffding's lemma (second-order expansion of the log-MGF) Hoeffding's lemma; KL local quadratic approximation \({\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+h})\approx\tfrac12h^\top F(\theta)h\) (Fisher information, natural gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence); asymptotic normality via the delta method.
cards.ex: Local behaviour of KL for softmax policies: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\theta+h})=\tfrac12h^\top F(\theta)h+O({\lVert h\rVert}^3)\), which is why TRPO's KL trust region is approximately a Fisher-norm ball.
cards.use: Descent lemmas, natural-gradient and trust-region analysis, local convergence of EM, MGF bounds, error expansions of discount-sensitive values.

cards.name: Fubini–Tonelli theorem (swapping sums/integrals)
cards.lay: You may swap the order of two integrals (or sums, or an integral and an expectation) when everything is non-negative (Tonelli) or absolutely integrable (Fubini). This licenses writing \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_t=\sum_t{\mathbb{E}}\).
cards.st: Let \(f\) be measurable on \(X\times Y\) with \(\sigma\)-finite measures. If \(f\ge0\) (Tonelli), or \(\int\!\!\int|f|<\infty\) (Fubini), then \[ \int_X\!\int_Yf(x,y)\,{\mathrm{d}}\nu(y){\mathrm{d}}\mu(x)=\int_Y\!\int_Xf(x,y)\,{\mathrm{d}}\mu(x){\mathrm{d}}\nu(y). \]
ver: Series form: \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tr_t=\sum_t\gamma^t{\mathbb{E}} r_t\) when rewards are bounded (dominated by \(\tfrac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\)).
Swapping sums: \(\sum_i\sum_ja_{ij}=\sum_j\sum_ia_{ij}\) if \(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|<\infty\).
Layer-cake / tail formula: \({\mathbb{E}} X=\int_0^\infty\Pr(X>t){\mathrm{d}} t\) for \(X\ge0\) is Tonelli applied to \({\mathbf{1}}\{t<X\}\) Tail-integral (layer-cake) formula.
cards.det: The occupancy-measure identity \(V^\pi(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_\rho}r(s,a)\) Discounted occupancy measures is a Fubini swap: \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_t\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)=\sum_{s,a}r(s,a)\sum_t\gamma^t\Pr(s_t=s,a_t=a)\).
cards.ex: Counter-example to remember: \(a_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\), \(-1\) if \(j=i+1\), else \(0\); row sums are \(0\) but column sums are not — swapping fails without absolute summability.
cards.use: Occupancy measures, policy-gradient derivations, tail-integral formulas, expectations of discounted returns, interchanging \({\mathbb{E}}\) and \(\sum\) in regret.

cards.name: Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral
cards.plain: Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral
cards.lay: The gradient of an expectation with respect to the distribution's parameters can be written as an expectation of (function \(\times\) gradient of log-density). This turns gradients into things you can estimate from samples, and is the root of REINFORCE and the Fisher identity in EM.
cards.st: If \(p_ heta\) is differentiable in \( heta\) and differentiation under the integral is justified (e.g. by dominated convergence Monotone & dominated convergence theorems): \[ abla_ heta{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim p_ heta}[f(x)]={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim p_ heta} igl[f(x) abla_ heta\log p_ heta(x) igr],\qquad {\mathbb{E}}_{p_ heta}[ abla_ heta\log p_ heta]=0. \]
ver: Baselines: \({\mathbb{E}}[(f(x)-b)\nabla\log p_\theta(x)]=\nabla{\mathbb{E}} f\) for any \(b\) not depending on \(x\) (variance reduction).
Trajectories: \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)=\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\) — dynamics cancel (model-free policy gradient Policy gradient theorem).
Leibniz rule: \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}\int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)}f(x,\theta){\mathrm{d}} x\) including boundary terms.
Reparameterisation alternative: if \(x=g_\theta({\varepsilon})\), \(\nabla{\mathbb{E}} f(x)={\mathbb{E}}[\nabla_\theta f(g_\theta({\varepsilon}))]\) (pathwise gradient).
Fisher identity in EM: \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)={\mathbb{E}}_{z\sim p_\theta(\cdot|x)}[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x,z)]\) Fisher's identity (score of the observed likelihood).
cards.det: Derivation. \( abla\int f p_ heta=\int f abla p_ heta=\int fp_ heta abla\log p_ heta\). The zero-mean property follows from \(f\equiv1\). The second moment \({\mathbb{E}}[ abla\log p\, abla\log p^ op]\) is the Fisher information, which defines the natural gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence.
cards.ex: REINFORCE: \(\nabla J(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}_\tau\bigl[\sum_t\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\,G_t\bigr]\) where \(G_t\) is the return from \(t\); subtracting \(V(s_t)\) (a baseline) keeps it unbiased.
cards.use: Policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE and actor-critic estimators, Fisher identity and gradient-EM, score-function gradients in variational inference.

cards.name: Monotone & dominated convergence theorems
cards.lay: When can you pass a limit inside an expectation? If the functions increase (monotone convergence), or if they are all bounded by one integrable function (dominated convergence). These justify infinite-horizon limits and differentiating under the expectation.
cards.st: (MCT) If \(0\le f_n\uparrow f\) pointwise then \(\int f_n\to\int f\). (DCT) If \(f_n\to f\) pointwise and \(|f_n|\le g\) with \(\int g<\infty\), then \(\int f_n\to\int f\).
ver: Fatou's lemma: \(\int\liminf f_n\le\liminf\int f_n\) for \(f_n\ge0\).
Bounded convergence: if \(|f_n|\le C\) on a finite measure space, DCT applies with \(g=C\).
Conditional versions hold for conditional expectations.
Uniform integrability: the sharp condition for \({\mathbb{E}} X_n\to{\mathbb{E}} X\) given \(X_n\to X\) in probability (Vitali).
cards.det: DCT is the technical backbone of differentiating under the integral sign Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral (needed for the policy gradient theorem with continuous actions) and of optional stopping Optional stopping theorem, where you need \({\mathbb{E}} X_{\tau\wedge n}\to{\mathbb{E}} X_\tau\).
cards.ex: \(V^\pi(s)=\lim_{H\to\infty}{\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t<H}\gamma^tr_t\): partial sums are dominated by \(\tfrac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\), so DCT allows the limit to be moved inside.
cards.use: Infinite-horizon limits, policy gradient regularity, optional stopping, convergence of EM iterates in expectation, average-reward limits.

cards.name: Danskin's theorem / envelope theorem
cards.lay: The derivative of an optimal value with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the objective at the optimum — you can ignore how the optimiser moves. Explains gradients of \(\max\) functions and of value functions.
cards.st: Let \(\phi(x)=\max_{z\in Z}f(x,z)\) with \(Z\) compact and \(f(\cdot,z)\) differentiable, \(f\), \( abla_xf\) continuous. Then \(\phi\) is directionally differentiable and its subdifferential is \[ \partial\phi(x)=\mathrm{conv}\{ abla_xf(x,z^\star):z^\star\in{\operatorname*{arg\,max}}_zf(x,z)\}. \] If the maximiser is unique, \( abla\phi(x)= abla_xf(x,z^\star(x))\).
ver: Envelope theorem (economics form): \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}\max_zf(z,\theta)=\partial_\theta f(z^\star,\theta)\).

Sensitivity of optimal value to rewards: \(\partial V^\star(\rho)/\partial r(s,a)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d^{\pi^\star}_\rho(s,a)\) when \(\pi^\star\) is unique (via the LP LP formulation of MDPs & its dual).
Min–max games: gradient of \(\min_y f(x,y)\) in \(x\) is \(\nabla_xf(x,y^\star(x))\) — used in GDA analyses for saddle points.
cards.det: In EM, the ELBO \(F(q,\theta)\) is maximised over \(q\) in the E-step; by the envelope theorem \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta F(q^\star_\theta,\theta)\) — another view of the Fisher identity Fisher's identity (score of the observed likelihood) and of why EM fixed points are stationary points of the likelihood.
cards.ex: Robust MDP: \(\phi(\theta)=\min_{P\in{\mathcal{P}}}V^{\pi_\theta}_P\); its gradient is the policy gradient evaluated in the worst-case model \(P^\star(\theta)\).
cards.use: Gradients of value functions w.r.t. rewards (inverse RL), robust/adversarial RL, Lagrangian methods in constrained MDPs, EM stationary-point arguments.

cards.name: Grönwall's inequality (continuous & discrete)
cards.lay: If a quantity grows at most in proportion to itself (plus a forcing term), it is bounded by the corresponding exponential. The discrete version controls accumulated errors in recursive estimates.
cards.st: (Integral form) If \(u(t)\le\alpha+\int_0^t\beta(s)u(s){\mathrm{d}} s\) with \(\beta\ge0\), then \(u(t)\le\alpha\exp\bigl(\int_0^t\beta\bigr)\). (Discrete) If \(u_{n+1}\le(1+b_n)u_n+a_n\) with \(a_n,b_n\ge0\), then \[ u_n\le\Bigl(u_0+\sum_{k<n}a_k\Bigr)\exp\Bigl(\sum_{k<n}b_k\Bigr). \]
ver: Differential form: \(u'\le\beta u\Rightarrow u(t)\le u(0)e^{\int_0^t\beta}\).
Contracting version: \(u_{n+1}\le(1-c_n)u_n+a_n\) with \(c_n\in[0,1]\) gives \(u_n\le u_0\prod_k(1-c_k)+\sum_k a_k\prod_{j>k}(1-c_j)\) — see Recursion lemmas for SA rates (Chung's lemma) for rates.
Bihari–LaSalle: nonlinear generalisation \(u'\le\beta\,w(u)\).
cards.det: Grönwall is central to the ODE method in stochastic approximation ODE method (Borkar–Meyn) & two-timescale SA: it bounds how far an interpolated noisy iterate drifts from the true ODE trajectory over a finite time window. The discrete version also controls error growth in multi-step model rollouts (compounding errors \(\propto(1+L{\varepsilon})^H\)).
cards.ex: Model rollouts: if the learned dynamics \(\hat f\) has one-step error \({\varepsilon}\) and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, the \(H\)-step state error satisfies \(e_{h+1}\le Le_h+{\varepsilon}\), so \(e_H\le{\varepsilon}\tfrac{L^H-1}{L-1}\) — exponential compounding unless \(L\le1\).
cards.use: ODE method for SA/TD/Q-learning, compounding errors in model-based RL, stability of continuous-time policy dynamics, tracking drifting targets.

cards.name: Implicit & inverse function theorems
cards.lay: If an equation \(F(x,y)=0\) has a non-degenerate solution, then near it \(y\) is a smooth function of \(x\), and its derivative is computable. Used to differentiate fixed points (e.g. \(\theta^\star\) of EM or of a Bellman equation) with respect to parameters.
cards.st: Let \(F:{\mathbb{R}}^n\times{\mathbb{R}}^m\to{\mathbb{R}}^m\) be \(C^1\) with \(F(x_0,y_0)=0\) and \(\partial_yF(x_0,y_0)\) invertible. Then near \(x_0\) there is a unique \(C^1\) map \(y(x)\) with \(F(x,y(x))=0\) and \[ Dy(x)=-[\partial_yF(x,y(x))]^{-1}\partial_xF(x,y(x)). \]
ver: Inverse function theorem: if \(Df(x_0)\) is invertible, \(f\) is a local \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Fixed points: if \(x=G(x,\theta)\) with \({\lVert \partial_xG\rVert}<1\), then \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} x^\star}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}=(I-\partial_xG)^{-1}\partial_\theta G\) — e.g. \(\tfrac{\partial V^\pi}{\partial\theta}=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\tfrac{\partial(r^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V)}{\partial\theta}\).
cards.det: Differentiating the Bellman fixed point in this way is another derivation of the policy gradient theorem Policy gradient theorem. Differentiating the EM fixed point \(\theta^\star=M(\theta^\star)\) shows the EM rate is governed by the Jacobian \(DM(\theta^\star)\), the fraction of missing information Missing-information principle (Louis) & EM's convergence rate.
cards.ex: Bilevel/meta-RL hypergradients: \( frac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\phi}L( heta^\star(\phi))\) with \( abla_ heta g( heta^\star,\phi)=0\) uses \(D heta^\star=-[ abla^2_ heta g]^{-1} abla^2_{ heta\phi}g\).
cards.use: Differentiating value fixed points, EM convergence rate, bilevel optimisation, sensitivity of equilibria in games.

cards.name: Union bound (Boole's inequality)
cards.lay: The chance that at least one of several bad things happens is at most the sum of their individual chances. It is crude but costs only a logarithm when combined with exponential tail bounds — the standard way to make a bound hold for all states, actions and times simultaneously.
cards.st: For any events \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) (finite or countable): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)\le\sum_i\Pr(A_i). \]
ver: Confidence splitting: to make \(N\) events each fail with total probability \(\le\delta\), allocate \(\delta/N\) to each; with Hoeffding this inflates widths by \(\sqrt{\log(N/\delta)}\) instead of \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}\).
Anytime split: allocate \(\delta_t=\tfrac{\delta}{t(t+1)}\) (sums to \(\delta\)) or \(\tfrac{6\delta}{\pi^2t^2}\) to cover all times \(t\ge1\).
Bonferroni inequalities: alternating partial inclusion–exclusion sums give upper/lower bounds.
Expectation form: \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iX_i\le\sum_i{\mathbb{E}} X_i^+\); for tails, \(\Pr(\max_iX_i>t)\le\sum_i\Pr(X_i>t)\) Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima.
cards.det: Union bounds are where the “\(\log\)” factors of RL come from. In tabular RL one typically unions over all \((s,a)\) pairs, all counts \(n\le T\), and sometimes all value functions in a finite set, giving \(\log(SAT/\delta)\). When the set is infinite (all value functions), one unions over a cover instead Covering & packing numbers (volumetric bound), or uses a chaining/martingale argument to avoid the loss.
cards.ex: For \(K\) arms, Hoeffding + union bound over arms and pulls \(n\le T\): with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), simultaneously for all \(a,n\): \(|\hat\mu_{a,n}-\mu_a|\le\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2KT/\delta)}{2n}}\).
cards.use: Every high-probability guarantee: uniform confidence sets over states/actions/time, finite-class generalisation, good-event arguments in regret analysis.

cards.name: Markov's inequality
cards.lay: A non-negative random variable is rarely much larger than its mean: it exceeds \(k\) times its mean with probability at most \(1/k\). Every other tail bound is Markov applied to a cleverly chosen function.
cards.st: For \(X\ge0\) and \(t>0\): \[ \Pr(X\ge t)\le\frac{{\mathbb{E}} X}{t}. \]
ver: For any non-decreasing \(\phi\ge0\): \(\Pr(X\ge t)\le\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)}{\phi(t)}\).
Chebyshev: \(\phi(x)=x^2\) applied to \(|X-{\mathbb{E}} X|\) Chebyshev's inequality (and Cantelli); Chernoff: \(\phi(x)=e^{\lambda x}\) Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method.
Expectation-to-high-probability: if \({\mathbb{E}}[{\mathrm{Reg}}]\le B\) then \(\Pr({\mathrm{Reg}}\ge B/\delta)\le\delta\) (poor \(1/\delta\) dependence).
Reverse Markov: if \(X\le M\) a.s. then \(\Pr(X>t)\ge\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}} X-t}{M-t}\) for \(t<{\mathbb{E}} X\).
cards.det:
Proof. \(t{\mathbf{1}}\{X\ge t\}\le X\); take expectations.
