Ville's inequality Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds) is the time-uniform analogue for non-negative supermartingales: the probability that the process ever exceeds \(1/\delta\) is at most \(\delta\) times its initial value.
cards.ex: A policy-evaluation estimator with \({\mathbb{E}}|\widehat V-V|\le{\varepsilon}\) satisfies \(|\widehat V-V|\le10{\varepsilon}\) with probability \(\ge0.9\); median-of-means boosts this to \(\log(1/\delta)\) dependence.
cards.use: Converting expectation bounds into probability bounds, deriving Chebyshev/Chernoff, median-of-means arguments, Ville's inequality for anytime-valid confidence sequences.

cards.name: Chebyshev's inequality (and Cantelli)
cards.lay: A random variable is unlikely to be many standard deviations from its mean: \(k\) standard deviations happens with probability at most \(1/k^2\). Requires only a finite variance.
cards.st: For \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and \(t>0\): \[ \Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}. \]
ver: Sample mean of \(n\) i.i.d. copies: \(\Pr(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge t)\le\tfrac{\sigma^2}{nt^2}\) (weak law of large numbers).
Cantelli (one-sided): \(\Pr(X-\mu\ge t)\le\tfrac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2}\).
Higher moments: \(\Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}}|X-\mu|^p}{t^p}\).

Median-of-means: split \(n\) samples into \(k\asymp\log(1/\delta)\) groups; the median of group means deviates by \(O(\sigma\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n})\) with probability \(1-\delta\) — sub-Gaussian behaviour from only finite variance.
cards.det: Chebyshev is weak in \(\delta\) (\(1/\sqrt\delta\) rather than \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}\)) but needs almost no assumptions. Median-of-means (Chebyshev for each block + a binomial/Hoeffding bound on how many blocks fail) is the standard robust alternative for heavy-tailed rewards, e.g. heavy-tailed bandits.
cards.ex: Importance-sampling off-policy estimates have finite but possibly huge variance \(\sigma^2\le{\mathbb{E}}[w^2]R_{\max}^2\); Chebyshev gives a valid (if loose) confidence interval without boundedness of the weights.
cards.use: Heavy-tailed bandits, robust mean estimation, quick sanity bounds, proving weak laws of large numbers.

cards.name: Jensen's inequality
cards.lay: For a convex function, the function of the average is at most the average of the function. Moving expectations inside or outside convex/concave functions is one of the most frequent proof steps in all of theory — and the reason the EM lower bound exists.
cards.st: If \(\phi\) is convex and \(X\), \(\phi(X)\) are integrable: \[ \phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\le{\mathbb{E}}\phi(X). \] For concave \(\phi\) the inequality reverses: \({\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)\le\phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\).
ver: Finite form: \(\phi(\sum_iw_ix_i)\le\sum_iw_i\phi(x_i)\) for weights \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum w_i=1\) (definition of convexity).
Conditional Jensen: \(\phi({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}])\le{\mathbb{E}}[\phi(X)\mid{\mathcal{F}}]\).

Common instances: \(({\mathbb{E}} X)^2\le{\mathbb{E}} X^2\); \({\mathbb{E}}\sqrt X\le\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} X}\); \({\mathbb{E}}\log X\le\log{\mathbb{E}} X\); \(e^{{\mathbb{E}} X}\le{\mathbb{E}} e^X\); \(|{\mathbb{E}} X|\le{\mathbb{E}}|X|\); \({\lVert {\mathbb{E}} X\rVert}\le{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert X\rVert}\).
EM/variational: \(\log p(x)=\log{\mathbb{E}}_{q}\bigl[\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\bigr]\ge{\mathbb{E}}_q\log\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\) — the ELBO ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM).
Gap control: \({\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)-\phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\le\tfrac{L}{2}{\operatorname{Var}} X\) for \(L\)-smooth \(\phi\); Jensen gap equals a Bregman divergence in expectation.
cards.det:
Proof. Convex \(\phi\) lies above a supporting line at \(\mu={\mathbb{E}} X\): \(\phi(x)\ge\phi(\mu)+g(x-\mu)\). Take expectations; the linear term vanishes.

Jensen proves: Gibbs' inequality \({\mathrm{KL}}\ge0\) KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality; the EM lower bound ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM); AM–GM AM–GM inequality; \({\mathbb{E}}\max\ge\max{\mathbb{E}}\) (optimism bias of maximising over noisy estimates — the reason Q-learning overestimates and double Q-learning exists).
cards.ex: Overestimation in Q-learning: \({\mathbb{E}}[\max_a\widehat Q(s,a)]\ge\max_a{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat Q(s,a)]=\max_aQ(s,a)\) when \(\widehat Q\) is unbiased, because \(\max\) is convex.
cards.use: ELBO/EM derivations, KL non-negativity, maximisation bias, converting second-moment bounds to first-moment bounds, convexity-based regret bounds, \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) of sums of variances.

cards.name: Tower property & law of total expectation
cards.plain: Tower property & law of total expectation
cards.lay: Averaging in stages gives the same answer as averaging all at once: first average over what you don't know given partial information, then average over the partial information. This is the probabilistic content of the Bellman equation.
cards.st: For integrable \(X\) and \(\sigma\)-algebras \({\mathcal{F}}_1\subseteq{\mathcal{F}}_2\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2]\bigm|{\mathcal{F}}_1\bigr]={\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1],\qquad{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]\bigr]={\mathbb{E}} X. \]
ver: Taking out what is known: \({\mathbb{E}}[ZX\mid{\mathcal{F}}]=Z{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}]\) if \(Z\) is \({\mathcal{F}}\)-measurable.
Bellman: \(V^\pi(s)={\mathbb{E}}[r_0+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}[G_1\mid s_1]\mid s_0=s]={\mathbb{E}}[r_0+\gamma V^\pi(s_1)\mid s_0=s]\) (Markov property + tower).
Law of total probability: \(\Pr(A)=\sum_i\Pr(A\mid B_i)\Pr(B_i)\).
Martingale differences: \({\mathbb{E}}[\xi_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]=0\Rightarrow{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_tZ_t\xi_t]=0\) for predictable \(Z_t\).
cards.det: Most regret proofs condition on the history \({\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\), bound a conditional expectation, then use the tower property to remove the conditioning. The difference between a quantity and its conditional expectation is a martingale difference — the starting point for Azuma/Freedman Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales), Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein).
cards.ex: Unbiasedness of the TD target given \(s\): \({\mathbb{E}}[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\mid s]=(T^\pi V^\pi)(s)=V^\pi(s)\), so \(\delta_t=r_t+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})-V^\pi(s_t)\) is a martingale difference sequence.
cards.use: Bellman equations, martingale constructions, regret decompositions, conditioning on good events, Wald's identity, EM's E-step.

cards.name: Change of measure / importance sampling identity
cards.plain: Change of measure / importance sampling identity
cards.lay: You can compute an average under distribution \(P\) using samples from \(Q\) by reweighting each sample by the likelihood ratio \(P/Q\). It underlies off-policy evaluation, the KL chain rule and most lower-bound proofs.
cards.st: If \(P\ll Q\) (absolute continuity) with Radon–Nikodym derivative \(w={\mathrm{d}} P/{\mathrm{d}} Q\), then for integrable \(f\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}_P[f(X)]={\mathbb{E}}_Q\bigl[w(X)f(X)\bigr]. \]
ver: Trajectory ratio: for policies \(\pi\) (target) and \(\mu\) (behaviour) in the same MDP, \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P^\pi}{{\mathrm{d}} P^\mu}(\tau)=\prod_t\tfrac{\pi(a_t|s_t)}{\mu(a_t|s_t)}\) — dynamics cancel.

Variance: \({\operatorname{Var}}_Q(wf)={\mathbb{E}}_P[wf^2]-({\mathbb{E}}_Pf)^2\le{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty^2(1+\chi^2(P\|Q))-({\mathbb{E}}_Pf)^2\) \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations.
Self-normalised IS: \(\hat\mu=\tfrac{\sum_iw_if(x_i)}{\sum_iw_i}\), biased but lower variance.

Lower-bound (likelihood-ratio) form: \(\Pr_P(A)={\mathbb{E}}_Q[w{\mathbf{1}}_A]\), so if \(w\) is not too small on \(A\), \(A\) is likely under \(P\) too — basis of the Lai–Robbins argument Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound.
Marginalised IS: using state-action occupancy ratios \(\tfrac{d^\pi(s,a)}{d^\mu(s,a)}\) instead of trajectory products avoids exponential-in-horizon variance.
cards.det: \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_P\log w\) and \(\chi^2(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_Qw^2-1\) are both expressed via the likelihood ratio, which is why these divergences control importance-sampling error. Trajectory-level IS weights have variance growing like \((\max\tfrac{\pi}{\mu})^{2H}\) — the curse of horizon in off-policy evaluation.
cards.ex: Off-policy evaluation: \(V^\pi={\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim\mu}\bigl[\prod_{t<H}\tfrac{\pi(a_t|s_t)}{\mu(a_t|s_t)}\sum_t r_t\bigr]\); per-decision IS uses only the prefix product up to \(t\) for reward \(r_t\).
cards.use: Off-policy evaluation, EXP3's importance-weighted loss estimates EXP3 & importance-weighted loss estimators, lower-bound constructions, Girsanov-type arguments, PPO/TRPO surrogate objectives.

cards.name: Law of total variance (and the variance of returns)
cards.plain: Law of total variance (and the variance of returns)
cards.lay: Total variance = average within-group variance + variance of the group means. In RL, applied recursively over time, it shows that the sum of per-step conditional variances of \(V\) equals the variance of the return — which is bounded by \(H^2\) rather than \(H^3\). This is the key to horizon-optimal bounds.
cards.st: For square-integrable \(X\) and any random variable \(Y\): \[ {\operatorname{Var}}(X)={\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid Y)\bigr]+{\operatorname{Var}}\bigl({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]\bigr). \]
ver: Finite-horizon RL (Azar et al., 2013/2017): \({\mathbb{E}}\Bigl[\sum_{h=1}^H{\operatorname{Var}}_{P_h(\cdot|s_h,a_h)}(V^\pi_{h+1})\Bigr]={\operatorname{Var}}\Bigl(\sum_hr_h\Bigr)\le H^2\) for rewards in \([0,1]\).

Discounted: \(\bigl\|(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\sigma_{V^\pi}\bigr\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{(1-\gamma)^3}}\) where \(\sigma_V(s)=\sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}}_{P(\cdot|s,\pi(s))}(V)}\) (Azar, Munos, Kappen 2013).

Conditional version: \({\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1)={\mathbb{E}}[{\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1]+{\operatorname{Var}}({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2]\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1)\).
cards.det: Naively each per-step variance is at most \(H^2\), so the sum over \(H\) steps is \(H^3\), leading to \(\sqrt{H^3}\) factors. The total-variance identity (applied to the return, with \(Y\) the history) shows the sum is in fact only \(H^2\) in expectation. Combined with Bernstein Bernstein's inequality or Freedman Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein) bonuses, this gives minimax-optimal \(\sqrt{H^2SAT}\)-type regret (UCBVI-Bernstein, Azar et al. 2017) and the \((1-\gamma)^{-3}\) sample complexity of model-based RL with a generative model.
cards.ex: Two-stage experiment: pick a coin with bias \(B\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0.2,0.8\}\), flip it. \({\operatorname{Var}}(X)={\mathbb{E}}[B(1-B)]+{\operatorname{Var}}(B)=0.16+0.09=0.25\), consistent with \(X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.5)\).
cards.use: Horizon-optimal regret and sample complexity (variance-aware bonuses), Bernstein-based confidence sets, variance of off-policy estimators, Bayesian variance decompositions.

cards.name: Tail-integral (layer-cake) formula
cards.lay: The mean of a non-negative variable is the area under its tail probability curve. It converts high-probability bounds (tails) into expectation bounds — e.g. a sub-Gaussian tail gives a \(\sqrt{\log}\) expected maximum.
cards.st: For \(X\ge0\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} X=\int_0^\infty\Pr(X>t)\,{\mathrm{d}} t,\qquad {\mathbb{E}} X^p=\int_0^\infty pt^{p-1}\Pr(X>t)\,{\mathrm{d}} t. \]
ver: Integer-valued: \({\mathbb{E}} N=\sum_{k\ge1}\Pr(N\ge k)\).
Split at a threshold: \({\mathbb{E}} X\le a+\int_a^\infty\Pr(X>t){\mathrm{d}} t\); with a high-probability bound \(\Pr(X>a+\sqrt{2\log(1/\delta)})\le\delta\) this gives \({\mathbb{E}} X\le a+O(1)\).
High-probability to expectation for regret: if \(\Pr({\mathrm{Reg}}>B\log(1/\delta))\le\delta\) for all \(\delta\) then \({\mathbb{E}}{\mathrm{Reg}}\le B(1+o(1))\).
cards.det: Proof. \(X=\int_0^\infty{\mathbf{1}}\{t<X\}{\mathrm{d}} t\); take expectations and use Tonelli Fubini–Tonelli theorem (swapping sums/integrals).
cards.ex: If \(\Pr(X>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}\) then \({\mathbb{E}} X\le\int_0^\infty2e^{-t^2/2}{\mathrm{d}} t=\sqrt{2\pi}\), i.e. \({\mathbb{E}} X=O(1)\); similarly for a maximum of \(n\) such variables one gets \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\).
cards.use: Converting high-probability regret bounds to expected regret, moment bounds for sub-Gaussian variables, expected hitting times.

cards.name: Popoviciu & Bhatia–Davis variance bounds
cards.lay: A random variable confined to \([a,b]\) has variance at most \((b-a)^2/4\) — attained by a fair coin on the endpoints. If you also know the mean, Bhatia–Davis gives a sharper bound.
cards.st: If \(a\le X\le b\) a.s. with mean \(\mu\): \[ {\operatorname{Var}}(X)\le(b-\mu)(\mu-a)\le\frac{(b-a)^2}{4}. \]
ver: Bernoulli: \({\operatorname{Var}}(X)=p(1-p)\le\tfrac14\); for \([0,1]\) variables \({\operatorname{Var}} X\le\mu(1-\mu)\le\mu\).
Value functions: \({\operatorname{Var}}_{s'\sim P}(V(s'))\le\tfrac{{\operatorname{sp}}(V)^2}{4}\le\tfrac{1}{4(1-\gamma)^2}\).
cards.det: Proof. \((b-X)(X-a)\ge0\), expand and take expectations: \({\mathbb{E}} X^2\le(a+b)\mu-ab\), so \({\operatorname{Var}} X\le(a+b)\mu-ab-\mu^2=(b-\mu)(\mu-a)\). This is the variance proxy implicitly used by Hoeffding's lemma Hoeffding's lemma.
cards.ex: Rewards in \([0,1]\) with small mean \(\mu\): \({\operatorname{Var}}\le\mu\), so Bernstein gives widths \(\sqrt{\mu\log(1/\delta)/n}\) instead of \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\) — the source of “small-loss” improvements.
cards.use: Variance proxies in Bernstein/empirical-Bernstein bonuses, small-loss bounds, sanity checks.

cards.name: Gaussian tail (Mills ratio) bounds
cards.lay: The standard normal tail \(\Pr(Z>t)\) decays like \(e^{-t^2/2}/t\). Precise two-sided bounds are needed for Gaussian lower-bound constructions and for analysing Thompson sampling.
cards.st: For \(Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) and \(t>0\): \[ \frac{t}{t^2+1}\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\le\Pr(Z>t)\le\frac{1}{t}\frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad\Pr(Z>t)\le\tfrac12e^{-t^2/2}. \]
ver: Chernoff form: \(\Pr(|Z|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}\).
Anti-concentration (needed for Thompson sampling optimism): \(\Pr(Z>t)\ge\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\tfrac{t}{t^2+1}e^{-t^2/2}\), so the posterior sample is optimistic with constant probability.
Expected maximum of \(n\) standard Gaussians: \(\sqrt{2\log n}-o(1)\le{\mathbb{E}}\max_iZ_i\le\sqrt{2\log n}\) Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima.
cards.det: Upper bound proof: \(\Pr(Z>t)=\int_t^\infty\phi(x){\mathrm{d}} x\le\int_t^\infty\tfrac{x}{t}\phi(x){\mathrm{d}} x=\tfrac{\phi(t)}{t}\). The lower bound uses \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}} x}\bigl[-\tfrac{x}{x^2+1}\phi(x)\bigr]\le\phi(x)\).
cards.ex: Thompson sampling for linear bandits (Agrawal–Goyal, Abeille–Lazaric): Gaussian anti-concentration ensures that a sampled parameter is optimistic with probability at least a constant \(p\approx0.15\), which drives the regret proof.
cards.use: Thompson sampling analyses, Gaussian bandit lower bounds, sub-Gaussian maximal inequalities, RLSVI randomised value functions.

cards.name: Borel–Cantelli lemmas
cards.lay: If the probabilities of a sequence of bad events are summable, then almost surely only finitely many of them happen. The standard route from high-probability bounds to almost-sure convergence.
cards.st: (First lemma) If \(\sum_n\Pr(A_n)<\infty\) then \(\Pr(A_n\text{ infinitely often})=0\). (Second lemma) If the \(A_n\) are independent and \(\sum_n\Pr(A_n)=\infty\), then \(\Pr(A_n\text{ i.o.})=1\).
ver: Conditional (Lévy) extension: for adapted events, \(\{A_n\text{ i.o.}\}=\{\sum_n\Pr(A_n\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{n-1})=\infty\}\) a.s.
Usage pattern: show \(\Pr(|X_n-X|>{\varepsilon})\le Cn^{-2}\), conclude \(X_n\to X\) a.s.
cards.det: First lemma proof: \(\Pr(\bigcup_{n\ge N}A_n)\le\sum_{n\ge N}\Pr(A_n)\to0\) (union bound + tail of a convergent series).
cards.ex: Infinite exploration in GLIE schemes: with \({\varepsilon}_t=1/t\), the events “explore action \(a\) at time \(t\)” have \(\sum_t{\varepsilon}_t/|{\mathcal{A}}|=\infty\), and the conditional second lemma shows every action is tried infinitely often a.s.
cards.use: Almost-sure convergence of Q-learning/SARSA (with SA theorems), GLIE conditions, consistency of estimators.

cards.name: Wald's identity
cards.lay: The expected sum of a random number of i.i.d. terms equals (expected number of terms) \(\times\) (expected term), provided the stopping decision doesn't peek into the future. Used to compute expected cumulative reward up to a stopping time.
cards.st: Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be i.i.d. with \({\mathbb{E}}|X_1|<\infty\) and \(N\) a stopping time with \({\mathbb{E}} N<\infty\). Then \[ {\mathbb{E}}\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^NX_i\Bigr]={\mathbb{E}} N\cdot{\mathbb{E}} X_1. \]
ver: Wald's second identity: if \({\mathbb{E}} X_1=0\), \({\mathbb{E}} X_1^2=\sigma^2\), then \({\mathbb{E}}\bigl(\sum_{i\le N}X_i\bigr)^2=\sigma^2{\mathbb{E}} N\).

Bandit regret identity: \({\mathbb{E}}{\mathrm{Reg}}_T=\sum_a\Delta_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\) is Wald-like (rewards of arm \(a\) are i.i.d., pulls are stopping-time determined) Regret decomposition (bandits).
Exponential (Wald martingale): \({\mathbb{E}}\bigl[e^{\lambda S_N}/M(\lambda)^N\bigr]=1\) under conditions — used for sequential tests.
cards.det: Proof via optional stopping Optional stopping theorem on the martingale \(S_n-n{\mathbb{E}} X_1\), or directly: \(\sum_{i\le N}X_i=\sum_iX_i{\mathbf{1}}\{N\ge i\}\), and \(\{N\ge i\}\) is independent of \(X_i\).
cards.ex: Expected number of steps to first success when each step succeeds with probability \(p\) is \(1/p\); expected total reward collected before success is \({\mathbb{E}} N\cdot{\mathbb{E}} r\).
cards.use: Bandit regret decomposition, sequential testing / best-arm identification lower bounds, expected cost-to-go in SSPs.

cards.name: Hoeffding's inequality
cards.lay: The average of \(n\) independent bounded random variables is within about \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\) of its mean, except with probability \(\delta\). The single most used inequality in bandits and RL.
cards.st: Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be independent with \(X_i\in[a_i,b_i]\) and \(S_n=\sum_iX_i\). For \(t>0\): \[ \Pr\bigl(S_n-{\mathbb{E}} S_n\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2}\Bigr). \] For i.i.d. \(X_i\in[0,1]\) with mean \(\mu\): with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), \(|\bar X_n-\mu|\le\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}\).
ver: Two-sided: multiply the bound by \(2\).
Range \([0,R]\) (e.g. returns in \([0,\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}]\)): width \(R\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}\).

Sub-Gaussian form: \(X_i\in[a,b]\) is \(\tfrac{b-a}{2}\)-sub-Gaussian Hoeffding's lemma; any sum of independent \(\sigma_i\)-sub-Gaussians obeys the same bound with \(\sum\sigma_i^2\) Sub-Gaussian random variables.
Martingale version: Azuma–Hoeffding Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales).
Functions of independent variables: McDiarmid McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality.
Sampling without replacement from a finite population: the same bound holds (Hoeffding 1963; Serfling gives an improvement).

KL (Chernoff–Hoeffding) form: \(\Pr(\bar X_n\ge\mu+t)\le e^{-n\,\mathrm{kl}(\mu+t,\mu)}\) for \([0,1]\)-valued variables, sharper than Hoeffding since \(\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\ge2(p-q)^2\) Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method.
cards.det:
Proof. Chernoff's method Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method: \(\Pr(S_n-{\mathbb{E}} S_n\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda t}\prod_i{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X_i-{\mathbb{E}} X_i)}\le e^{-\lambda t+\lambda^2\sum(b_i-a_i)^2/8}\) by Hoeffding's lemma; optimise \(\lambda=4t/\sum(b_i-a_i)^2\).

Limitation: Hoeffding ignores variance. If \({\operatorname{Var}} X_i\ll(b-a)^2\), Bernstein Bernstein's inequality is much sharper. Also, Hoeffding needs independence or a fixed sample size: in bandits the number of pulls \(N_a(t)\) is random, which is handled either by a union bound over all possible counts \(n\le T\) or by martingale/time-uniform bounds Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds).
cards.ex: UCB1: for each arm, \(\hat\mu_a+\sqrt{\tfrac{2\log t}{N_a}}\) upper-bounds \(\mu_a\) with probability \(\ge1-t^{-4}\) (union over \(N_a\le t\) costs a factor \(t\)).
cards.use: UCB bonuses, Hoeffding-based tabular RL (UCBVI-Hoeffding, Q-learning with UCB), Monte-Carlo policy evaluation, PAC bounds for finite classes, model estimation.

cards.name: Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method
cards.lay: To bound a tail, exponentiate: apply Markov's inequality to \(e^{\lambda X}\) and optimise over \(\lambda\). Exponential moments of sums of independent variables factorise, so tails of sums decay exponentially. Gives the exact large-deviation rate, which is a KL divergence.
cards.st: For any random variable \(X\) and \(t\): \[ \Pr(X\ge t)\le\inf_{\lambda>0}e^{-\lambda t}{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X}=\exp\bigl(-\psi^*(t)\bigr),\quad\psi^*(t)=\sup_{\lambda>0}\{\lambda t-\log{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X}\}. \] For i.i.d. sums, \(\Pr(\bar X_n\ge t)\le e^{-n\psi^*_{X_1}(t)}\).
ver: Bernoulli / KL form: for i.i.d. \(X_i\in\{0,1\}\) (or \([0,1]\)) with mean \(p\) and \(q>p\): \(\Pr(\bar X_n\ge q)\le\exp(-n\,\mathrm{kl}(q,p))\) where \(\mathrm{kl}(q,p)=q\log\tfrac qp+(1-q)\log\tfrac{1-q}{1-p}\). Basis of KL-UCB.
Gaussian: \(\psi^*(t)=\tfrac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\), giving \(\Pr(\bar X_n-\mu\ge t)\le e^{-nt^2/(2\sigma^2)}\).
Multiplicative forms for sums of Bernoullis: see Multiplicative Chernoff bounds.
Cramér's theorem: the bound is tight on the exponential scale, \(\tfrac1n\log\Pr(\bar X_n\ge t)\to-\psi^*(t)\).
Sanov's theorem: empirical distributions deviate to a set \(\Gamma\) with probability \(\approx e^{-n\inf_{Q\in\Gamma}{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)}\).
cards.det: All exponential concentration inequalities (Hoeffding, Bernstein, Bennett, sub-Gaussian/sub-exponential tails) are Chernoff's method plus a bound on the log-MGF. The optimal rate \(\psi^*\) is the Legendre transform of the log-MGF Convex conjugate & Fenchel–Young; for exponential families it equals a KL divergence. This is why KL appears both in upper bounds (KL-UCB) and lower bounds (Lai–Robbins Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound): they are two sides of the same large-deviation rate.
cards.ex: KL-UCB index: \(U_a(t)=\max\{q\in[0,1]:N_a\,\mathrm{kl}(\hat\mu_a,q)\le\log t+c\log\log t\}\). It is asymptotically optimal for Bernoulli bandits, matching Lai–Robbins.
cards.use: Deriving every exponential tail bound, KL-UCB and its RL analogues (KL-UCRL), large-deviation lower bounds, best-arm identification.

cards.name: Hoeffding's lemma
cards.lay: A bounded random variable has a moment generating function no bigger than that of a Gaussian with standard deviation equal to half its range. In other words, bounded \(\Rightarrow\) sub-Gaussian.
cards.st: If \(X\in[a,b]\) a.s. then for all \(\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-{\mathbb{E}} X)}\le\exp\Bigl(\frac{\lambda^2(b-a)^2}{8}\Bigr). \]
ver: Conditional version: if \(X\in[A,B]\) with \(A,B\) \({\mathcal{F}}\)-measurable, \({\mathbb{E}}[e^{\lambda(X-{\mathbb{E}}[X|{\mathcal{F}}])}\mid{\mathcal{F}}]\le e^{\lambda^2(B-A)^2/8}\) (used for Azuma Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales)).
Equivalently: \(X\) is \(\tfrac{b-a}{2}\)-sub-Gaussian Sub-Gaussian random variables.

Variance-sensitive refinement (Bennett/Bernstein MGF bound): \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le\exp\bigl(\tfrac{\sigma^2}{b^2}(e^{\lambda b}-1-\lambda b)\bigr)\) for \(X-\mu\le b\) Bennett's inequality.
cards.det: Proof idea. Let \(\psi(\lambda)=\log{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\); then \(\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0\) and \(\psi''(\lambda)\) is the variance of \(X\) under an exponentially tilted law, which is supported in \([a,b]\), hence \(\le(b-a)^2/4\) by Popoviciu Popoviciu & Bhatia–Davis variance bounds. Taylor Taylor's theorem with remainder gives \(\psi(\lambda)\le\lambda^2(b-a)^2/8\).
cards.ex: Rademacher \({\varepsilon}\in\{\pm1\}\): \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda{\varepsilon}}=\cosh\lambda\le e^{\lambda^2/2}\), matching the lemma with \(b-a=2\).
cards.use: Hoeffding and Azuma inequalities, sub-Gaussianity of bounded rewards and TD errors, PAC-Bayes bounds with bounded losses, exponential-weights analyses.

cards.name: Sub-Gaussian random variables
cards.lay: A random variable is sub-Gaussian if its tails are at least as light as a Gaussian's. Bounded, Gaussian, and Rademacher variables all qualify. Sums of independent sub-Gaussians are sub-Gaussian with variance proxies adding up — so one theory covers them all.
cards.st: \(X\) (mean \(\mu\)) is \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian if \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\) for all \(\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}\). Then \[ \Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \] and if \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are independent \(\sigma_i\)-sub-Gaussian, \(\sum_iX_i\) is \(\sqrt{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}\)-sub-Gaussian.
ver: Equivalent characterisations (up to constants): tails \(\Pr(|X|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/K_1^2}\); moments \(({\mathbb{E}}|X|^p)^{1/p}\le K_2\sqrt p\); \(\psi_2\)-norm \({\mathbb{E}} e^{X^2/K_3^2}\le2\) (Vershynin, Prop. 2.5.2).

Conditionally sub-Gaussian noise \({\mathbb{E}}[e^{\lambda\eta_t}|{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\le e^{\lambda^2R^2/2}\) is the standard assumption in linear bandits Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.).
Squares of sub-Gaussians are sub-exponential Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition.
Weighted sums: \(\sum_ia_iX_i\) is \({\lVert a\rVert}_2\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian (for i.i.d. \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian \(X_i\)).
cards.det: Sub-Gaussianity is closed under sums and scaling and gives Hoeffding-type bounds immediately. Most bandit and RL papers assume conditionally \(R\)-sub-Gaussian noise because it includes bounded and Gaussian rewards simultaneously. Beware: the variance proxy \(\sigma^2\) can be much larger than the true variance (e.g. a Bernoulli\((p)\) with tiny \(p\) has variance \(\approx p\) but optimal proxy \(\approx\tfrac{1}{4\log(1/p)}\)) — use Bernstein when variance matters.
cards.ex: Gaussian rewards \({\mathcal{N}}(\mu,1)\) and \([0,1]\)-bounded rewards are 1- and \(\tfrac12\)-sub-Gaussian respectively; UCB with bonus \(\sqrt{2\sigma^2\log(1/\delta)/n}\) works for both.
cards.use: Noise assumptions in bandits/linear MDPs, maximal inequalities, covering-number arguments, random-features analyses, Thompson sampling.

cards.name: Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima
cards.lay: The largest of \(n\) sub-Gaussian variables is typically only about \(\sigma\sqrt{2\log n}\) — the price of taking a max over many noisy quantities grows very slowly. This is why union bounds over huge (but finite) sets are cheap.
cards.st: If \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are each (not necessarily independent) zero-mean \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian: \[ {\mathbb{E}}\max_{i\le n}X_i\le\sigma\sqrt{2\log n},\qquad{\mathbb{E}}\max_{i\le n}|X_i|\le\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2n)}, \] and \(\Pr(\max_iX_i\ge\sigma\sqrt{2\log n}+t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}\).
ver: Finite-class uniform deviation: \({\mathbb{E}}\sup_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}(\hat{\mathbb{E}}_nf-{\mathbb{E}} f)\le\sqrt{\tfrac{\log|{\mathcal{F}}|}{2n}}\) for \([0,1]\)-valued \(f\) (each deviation is \(\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt n}\)-sub-Gaussian) — see Finite-class uniform convergence (Occam bound) and Massart Massart's finite class lemma.
Infinite sets: replace \(\log n\) by metric entropy and chain (Dudley Dudley's entropy integral (chaining)).
Gaussian lower bound: for i.i.d. \({\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\), \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iZ_i\ge c\sqrt{\log n}\) (Sudakov minoration for general Gaussian processes).
cards.det: Proof. For \(\lambda>0\), Jensen Jensen's inequality: \(e^{\lambda{\mathbb{E}}\max X_i}\le{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda\max X_i}\le\sum_i{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X_i}\le ne^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\). Hence \({\mathbb{E}}\max X_i\le\tfrac{\log n}{\lambda}+\tfrac{\lambda\sigma^2}{2}\); optimise \(\lambda=\sqrt{2\log n}/\sigma\). This is exactly the log-sum-exp trick Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
cards.ex: Maximisation bias in Q-learning: with \(A\) actions and \({\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2)\) noise on each \(\widehat Q(s,a)\), the \(\max_a\) overestimates by up to \(\sigma\sqrt{2\log A}\).
cards.use: Maximisation bias, finite-class generalisation, expected regret of follow-the-perturbed-leader, Rademacher complexity of finite classes, lower bounds via Sudakov.

cards.name: Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales)
cards.lay: Hoeffding's inequality still holds when the terms are not independent, as long as each new term has zero mean given the past and is bounded. This is what you need for adaptively collected data — i.e. every online RL algorithm.
cards.st: Let \((M_t)\) be a martingale with differences \(D_t=M_t-M_{t-1}\) satisfying \(A_t\le D_t\le B_t\) where \(A_t,B_t\) are \({\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\)-measurable with \(B_t-A_t\le c_t\). Then \[ \Pr(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^nc_i^2}\Bigr). \]
ver: Symmetric bounded differences \(|D_t|\le c_t\): \(\Pr(|M_n-M_0|\ge t)\le2\exp\bigl(-\tfrac{t^2}{2\sum c_i^2}\bigr)\).
Maximal version: the same bound holds for \(\Pr(\max_{k\le n}(M_k-M_0)\ge t)\) (via Doob/Ville Doob's maximal inequalities).
Conditionally sub-Gaussian differences: replace \(c_i^2/4\) by \(\sigma_i^2\).
Variance-aware version: Freedman Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein).
cards.det:
Proof. Chernoff + conditional Hoeffding lemma Hoeffding's lemma applied iteratively with the tower property Tower property & law of total expectation: \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(M_n-M_0)}={\mathbb{E}}\bigl[e^{\lambda(M_{n-1}-M_0)}{\mathbb{E}}[e^{\lambda D_n}|{\mathcal{F}}_{n-1}]\bigr]\le e^{\lambda^2c_n^2/8}{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(M_{n-1}-M_0)}\).

Typical RL martingales: \(\xi_t=(P_{s_t,a_t}-{\mathbf{1}}_{s_{t+1}})^\top V_{t+1}\) (transition noise against a predictable value function) and \(\Delta_t={\mathbb{E}}[\cdot\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]-(\text{realised})\) in regret decompositions.
cards.ex: In UCBVI-style regret proofs, the term \(\sum_{k,h}\bigl[(P(\cdot|s_h^k,a_h^k))^\top(V^\star_{h+1}-V^{\pi_k}_{h+1})-(V^\star_{h+1}-V^{\pi_k}_{h+1})(s_{h+1}^k)\bigr]\) is a martingale with increments bounded by \(H\), so Azuma bounds it by \(H\sqrt{2T\log(1/\delta)}\).
cards.use: Regret decompositions in online RL, Q-learning error terms, concentration of returns, McDiarmid's proof, adaptive data in bandits.

cards.name: Bernstein's inequality
cards.lay: Like Hoeffding, but uses the variance: the deviation is about \(\sqrt{\sigma^2\log(1/\delta)/n}+b\log(1/\delta)/n\). When variance is small (rare rewards, low-noise transitions) this is far sharper — and it is the gateway to horizon-optimal RL bounds.
cards.st: Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be independent with \({\mathbb{E}} X_i=\mu_i\), \(|X_i-\mu_i|\le b\) and \(\sum_i{\operatorname{Var}} X_i\le n\sigma^2\). Then for \(t>0\): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu_i)\ge t\Bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2+\tfrac23bt}\Bigr). \] Equivalently, with probability \(\ge1-\delta\): \(\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu_i)\le\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma^2\log(1/\delta)}{n}}+\frac{2b\log(1/\delta)}{3n}\).
ver: One-sided bound needs only \(X_i-\mu_i\le b\).

Moment (Bernstein) condition: \({\mathbb{E}}|X_i-\mu_i|^k\le\tfrac{k!}{2}\sigma^2b^{k-2}\) for \(k\ge2\) suffices (allows unbounded, sub-exponential variables Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition).
Martingale version: Freedman Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein). Empirical variance version: Empirical Bernstein inequality (Maurer–Pontil; Audibert et al.).
Sharper exponent: Bennett Bennett's inequality.
cards.det: Two regimes: for small \(t\) the tail is Gaussian with the true variance \(\sigma^2\); for large \(t\) it is exponential with scale \(b\). In RL, applying Bernstein to \(\widehat P^\top V\) gives widths \(\sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}}_P(V)\log/n}+\tfrac{H\log}{n}\); the total-variance identity Law of total variance (and the variance of returns) then shows \(\sum{\operatorname{Var}}_P(V)\) is only \(H^2\) over an episode, eliminating a \(\sqrt H\) factor compared to Hoeffding.
cards.ex: Rewards in \([0,1]\) with mean \(\mu=0.01\): Hoeffding gives width \(\approx\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)}\); Bernstein (with \(\sigma^2\le\mu\)) gives \(\approx\sqrt{0.02\log(1/\delta)/n}+\tfrac{2\log(1/\delta)}{3n}\) — roughly \(5\times\) smaller for moderate \(n\).
cards.use: Variance-aware bonuses (UCBVI-Bernstein, EULER, MVP), minimax sample complexity with a generative model, small-loss bounds, importance-sampling estimators with small variance.

cards.name: \(\ell_1\) deviation of the empirical distribution (Weissman et al.)
cards.plain: ℓ_1 deviation of the empirical distribution (Weissman et al.)
cards.lay: How close is an empirical distribution over \(S\) outcomes to the true one, in total variation? About \(\sqrt{S/n}\). This is the concentration bound behind UCRL2 and most model-based tabular RL analyses.
cards.st: Let \(\hat p\) be the empirical distribution of \(n\) i.i.d. samples from \(p\) on \(S\) outcomes. For \({\varepsilon}>0\): \[ \Pr\bigl({\lVert \hat p-p\rVert}_1\ge{\varepsilon}\bigr)\le(2^S-2)e^{-n{\varepsilon}^2/2}. \] Hence with probability \(\ge1-\delta\): \({\lVert \hat p-p\rVert}_1\le\sqrt{\frac{2\bigl(S\log2+\log(1/\delta)\bigr)}{n}}\).
ver: Expectation: \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \hat p-p\rVert}_1\le\sqrt{\tfrac{S-1}{n}}\) (by Cauchy–Schwarz on \(\sum_i\sqrt{p_i(1-p_i)/n}\)).

Avoiding the \(\sqrt S\): for a fixed vector \(V\), \(|(\hat p-p)^\top V|\lesssim{\operatorname{sp}}(V)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\) by Hoeffding — the reason optimal algorithms concentrate \(\widehat P^\top V^\star\) rather than \(\widehat P\) itself.

KL version (method of types): \(\Pr({\mathrm{KL}}(\hat p\|p)\ge{\varepsilon})\le(n+1)^{S}e^{-n{\varepsilon}}\); refined bounds \(\approx e^{-n{\varepsilon}}\cdot\mathrm{poly}\) (Agrawal 2020, Mardia et al.).
Bernstein-style per-coordinate: \(|\hat p(s')-p(s')|\le\sqrt{2p(s')\log(1/\delta)/n}+\tfrac{2\log(1/\delta)}{3n}\).
cards.det:
Proof idea. \({\lVert \hat p-p\rVert}_1=2\max_{A\subseteq[S]}(\hat p(A)-p(A))\); apply Hoeffding to each of the \(2^S-2\) non-trivial subsets and union bound Union bound (Boole's inequality).

Used with Hölder Hölder's inequality in the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error): \(|(\hat p-p)^\top V|\le{\lVert \hat p-p\rVert}_1{\lVert V\rVert}_\infty\), giving regret \({\widetilde{O}}(DS\sqrt{AT})\) for UCRL2. The extra \(\sqrt S\) (vs. the optimal \(\sqrt{SAT}\)-type bound) comes precisely from this step.
cards.ex: UCRL2 confidence set: \(\{\widetilde P:{\lVert \widetilde P(\cdot|s,a)-\widehat P(\cdot|s,a)\rVert}_1\le\sqrt{\tfrac{14S\log(2At/\delta)}{\max(1,N_t(s,a))}}\}\).
cards.use: Model-based tabular RL (UCRL2, PSRL analyses), robust MDP uncertainty sets, plug-in estimation, distribution testing.

cards.name: Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.)
cards.plain: Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.)
cards.lay: For least squares with adaptively chosen inputs and sub-Gaussian noise, the estimation error measured in the data's own geometry (\({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_{V_t}\)) is bounded uniformly over time by \(\sqrt{d\log t}\). This is the confidence ellipsoid used by LinUCB/OFUL and linear-MDP algorithms.
cards.st: Let \(x_t\in{\mathbb{R}}^d\) be \({\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\)-measurable, \(\eta_t\) conditionally \(R\)-sub-Gaussian, \(V_t=\lambda I+\sum_{s\le t}x_sx_s^\top\), \(S_t=\sum_{s\le t}\eta_sx_s\). With probability \(\ge1-\delta\), for all \(t\ge0\): \[ {\lVert S_t\rVert}^2_{V_t^{-1}}\le2R^2\log\Bigl(\frac{\det(V_t)^{1/2}\det(\lambda I)^{-1/2}}{\delta}\Bigr). \] Consequently, for ridge regression \(\hat\theta_t\) with \({\lVert \theta^\star\rVert}_2\le S\): \[ {\lVert \hat\theta_t-\theta^\star\rVert}_{V_t}\le R\sqrt{2\log\frac{\det(V_t)^{1/2}\lambda^{-d/2}}{\delta}}+\sqrt\lambda\,S. \]
ver: With \({\lVert x_t\rVert}\le L\): \(\log\tfrac{\det V_t}{\det\lambda I}\le d\log(1+tL^2/(d\lambda))\) Matrix determinant lemma, so the radius is \(\beta_t=R\sqrt{d\log\tfrac{1+tL^2/\lambda}{\delta}}+\sqrt\lambda S\).
Scalar version (Laplace method): w.p. \(1-\delta\), \(\forall t\): \(|S_t|\le\sqrt{2(1+V_t)\log(\sqrt{1+V_t}/\delta)}\) with \(V_t=\sum x_s^2\) (anytime Hoeffding).
Function-valued / kernel versions: Chowdhury & Gopalan (2017) for RKHS; vector-valued versions for linear MDPs with covering over value functions (Jin et al. 2020).
cards.det:
Proof idea (method of mixtures). For each fixed \(x\in{\mathbb{R}}^d\), \(M_t^x=\exp({\langle x, S_t\rangle}/R-\tfrac12{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V_t-\lambda I})\) is a non-negative supermartingale. Integrating over \(x\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\lambda^{-1}I)\) gives another supermartingale whose value is a closed-form Gaussian integral; Ville's inequality Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds) then gives a bound holding for all \(t\) simultaneously, without a union bound over time.

Combined with Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the \(V_t\) geometry and the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma, it yields OFUL regret \({\widetilde{O}}(d\sqrt T)\).
cards.ex: Linear bandit step: \({\langle x, \hat\theta_t-\theta^\star\rangle}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}{\lVert \hat\theta_t-\theta^\star\rVert}_{V_t}\le\beta_t{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\), so \({\langle x, \hat\theta_t\rangle}+\beta_t{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\) is an upper confidence bound for all \(x,t\).
cards.use: LinUCB/OFUL, LSVI-UCB in linear MDPs, GP-UCB, generalised linear bandits, non-stationary linear bandits with sliding windows/discounting (weighted \(V_t\)).

cards.name: Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein)
cards.lay: Bernstein's inequality for martingales: the deviation of a sum of martingale differences scales with the square root of the accumulated conditional variance, not the worst-case range. Essential for variance-aware online RL.
cards.st: Let \(D_t\) be martingale differences with \(D_t\le b\) a.s., and \(W_n=\sum_{t\le n}{\mathbb{E}}[D_t^2\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\). For all \(t,\sigma^2>0\): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\exists n:\ \sum_{s\le n}D_s\ge t\ \text{and}\ W_n\le\sigma^2\Bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{t^2}{2(\sigma^2+bt/3)}\Bigr). \]
ver: Random-variance form (peeling over dyadic levels of \(W_n\)): with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), for all \(n\) (with \(W_n\le nb^2\)), \(\sum_{t\le n}D_t\le c\bigl(\sqrt{W_n\iota_n}+b\,\iota_n\bigr)\) where \(\iota_n=\log\tfrac{\log(en)}{\delta}\) and \(c\) is a universal constant.

Self-bounding version: if \({\mathbb{E}}[D_t^2|{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\le b\,{\mathbb{E}}[Y_t|{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\) for non-negative \(Y_t\) one gets multiplicative bounds such as \(\sum_t{\mathbb{E}}[Y_t|{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\le2\sum_tY_t+O(b\log(1/\delta))\).
cards.det: Freedman's random-variance form is what you need when the variance proxy is itself data-dependent (e.g. \(\sum_t{\operatorname{Var}}_P(V^{\pi_k})\) along the trajectory). The usual trick: peel over geometric grids of \(W_n\) and union bound, costing a \(\log\log\) factor. Combined with the self-bounding inversion lemma Inverting \(x \le a + b\sqrt{x}\) and \(x \le a\log x\) it yields “first-order” bounds.
cards.ex: Multiplicative concentration of counts: if \(Y_t\in[0,1]\) then w.p. \(\ge1-\delta\), \(\sum_t{\mathbb{E}}[Y_t|{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]\le2\sum_tY_t+4\log(1/\delta)\) — used to show visit counts are at least half their expectation.
cards.use: Horizon-free and variance-dependent regret in tabular RL, concentration of visit counts, martingale analyses of Q-learning variance.

cards.name: Empirical Bernstein inequality (Maurer–Pontil; Audibert et al.)
cards.plain: Empirical Bernstein inequality (Maurer–Pontil; Audibert et al.)
cards.lay: Bernstein needs the true variance, which you don't know. Empirical Bernstein replaces it with the sample variance at a small extra cost \(\propto\log(1/\delta)/n\), giving fully data-driven, variance-adaptive confidence intervals.
cards.st: (Maurer & Pontil, 2009) For i.i.d. \(X_1,\dots,X_n\in[0,1]\), \(n\ge2\), with sample variance \(\widehat V_n=\tfrac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}(X_i-X_j)^2\), with probability \(\ge1-\delta\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} X-\bar X_n\le\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat V_n\log(2/\delta)}{n}}+\frac{7\log(2/\delta)}{3(n-1)}. \]
ver: Audibert, Munos & Szepesvári (2009) version: \(|\bar X_n-\mu|\le\sqrt{\tfrac{2\widehat V_n\log(3/\delta)}{n}}+\tfrac{3b\log(3/\delta)}{n}\) for range \(b\) (used in UCB-V).
Uniform over a finite class (with \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\)) and over covering numbers (Maurer–Pontil sample-variance penalisation).
Time-uniform empirical Bernstein confidence sequences (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 2024) via betting martingales Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds).
cards.det: The proof applies Bernstein to the mean and a separate concentration bound to the sample variance (\(\sqrt{\widehat V_n}\) concentrates around \(\sigma\) at rate \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\), a self-bounding property). In RL, bonuses of the form \(\sqrt{\widehat{{\operatorname{Var}}}_{\widehat P}(\widehat V)\,L/n}+HL/n\) are empirical-Bernstein bonuses; the analysis must also control the gap between \({\operatorname{Var}}_{\widehat P}(\widehat V)\) and \({\operatorname{Var}}_P(V^\star)\).
cards.ex: UCB-V: index \(\hat\mu+\sqrt{2\widehat V\log t/n}+3\log t/n\), which adapts to low-variance arms and improves regret when \(\sigma_a^2\ll1\).
cards.use: Variance-adaptive bandits (UCB-V), Bernstein-style bonuses in tabular RL (UCBVI-BF, EULER), sample-variance penalisation in offline policy selection.

cards.name: McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality
cards.lay: Any function of many independent inputs that can't change much when one input changes is concentrated around its mean. Generalises Hoeffding from sums to arbitrary “stable” functions such as suprema of empirical processes.
cards.st: Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be independent and \(f\) satisfy \(|f(x)-f(x')|\le c_i\) whenever \(x,x'\) differ only in coordinate \(i\). Then \[ \Pr\bigl(f(X)-{\mathbb{E}} f(X)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_ic_i^2}\Bigr). \]
ver: Uniform deviation: for \(f=\sup_{h\in{\mathcal{H}}}({\mathbb{E}} h-\hat{\mathbb{E}}_nh)\) with \(h\in[0,1]\), \(c_i=1/n\), so \(f\le{\mathbb{E}} f+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)}\) — then bound \({\mathbb{E}} f\) by Rademacher complexity Symmetrisation & Rademacher complexity bounds.
Variance version: Efron–Stein Efron–Stein inequality bounds the variance by the same bounded differences.
Markov-dependent data: versions via coupling/mixing times (e.g. Paulin 2015) Concentration for Markov chains (Paulin; Lezaud).
cards.det: Proof. Doob martingale \(M_k={\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid X_1,\dots,X_k]\) has differences in an interval of length \(c_k\); apply Azuma Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales).
cards.ex: Generalisation of an empirical-risk minimiser over a value-function class: McDiarmid reduces \(\sup_{f}|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_n\ell_f-{\mathbb{E}}\ell_f|\) to its expectation, which symmetrisation bounds by \(2\mathfrak R_n\).
cards.use: Uniform convergence / Rademacher bounds, stability-based generalisation, concentration of empirical Bellman errors, random-graph arguments.

cards.name: Multiplicative Chernoff bounds
cards.lay: For sums of independent \([0,1]\) variables with mean \(\mu\), the relative deviation shrinks like \(1/\sqrt\mu\). Perfect for statements like “a state visited with probability \(p\) is visited at least \(np/2\) times”.
cards.st: Let \(X=\sum_iX_i\) with independent \(X_i\in[0,1]\) and \(\mu={\mathbb{E}} X\). For \(\delta\in(0,1)\): \[ \Pr(X\le(1-\delta)\mu)\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/2},\qquad\Pr(X\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/3}, \] and for any \(\delta>0\): \(\Pr(X\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le\bigl(\tfrac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}}\bigr)^\mu\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/(2+\delta)}\).
ver: Half-mean bound: \(\Pr(X<\mu/2)\le e^{-\mu/8}\).
Large deviations: \(\Pr(X\ge t)\le2^{-t}\) for \(t\ge6\mu\).
Martingale/adaptive version: Freedman's self-bounding form Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein).
cards.det: Derived from Chernoff's method Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method using \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X_i}\le e^{\mu_i(e^\lambda-1)}\) (since \(1+x\le e^x\) Exponential bounds: \(1+x\le e^x\) and friends). Multiplicative bounds are crucial when \(\mu\) is small: additive Hoeffding would require \(n\gtrsim1/p^2\) samples to see a probability-\(p\) event, while multiplicative Chernoff shows \(n\gtrsim\log(1/\delta)/p\) suffices.
cards.ex: Reward-free exploration / coverage: a state with visitation probability \(p\) per episode is visited at least \(Kp/2\) times in \(K\) episodes w.p. \(\ge1-e^{-Kp/8}\).
cards.use: Visit-count lower bounds in tabular RL, load balancing, random sampling arguments, “significant states” analyses.

cards.name: Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds)
cards.plain: Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds)
cards.lay: A non-negative supermartingale that starts at 1 ever reaches \(1/\delta\) with probability at most \(\delta\). This gives confidence bounds that hold simultaneously for all times — no union bound over \(t\), and valid under optional stopping.
cards.st: If \((M_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a non-negative supermartingale, then for any \(c>0\): \[ \Pr\bigl(\exists t\ge0:\ M_t\ge c\bigr)\le\frac{{\mathbb{E}} M_0}{c}. \]
ver: Exponential supermartingales: for \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian increments, \(M_t^\lambda=\exp(\lambda S_t-\lambda^2t\sigma^2/2)\); mixing over \(\lambda\) yields \(|S_t|\le\sigma\sqrt{2(t+\rho)\log\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt{(t+\rho)/\rho}}{\delta}\bigr)}\) for all \(t\) (normal mixture boundary).
Confidence sequences: sets \(C_t\) with \(\Pr(\forall t:\theta\in C_t)\ge1-\delta\) (Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, Sekhon 2021).
Betting / e-processes: wealth of a gambler betting against \(H_0\) is a non-negative supermartingale; Ville makes “wealth \(\ge1/\delta\)” a valid test at any stopping time.
Discrete-time Doob maximal inequality is the special case for finite horizons Doob's maximal inequalities.
cards.det: Ville is Markov's inequality Markov's inequality for the whole path, proved via optional stopping Optional stopping theorem at the first time \(M_t\ge c\). The self-normalised bound Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.) is Ville applied to a Gaussian mixture of exponential supermartingales.
cards.ex: Adaptive stopping in A/B tests or best-arm identification: with a confidence sequence you may stop whenever the interval excludes 0, with error \(\le\delta\), despite peeking at every step.
cards.use: Anytime-valid confidence sets for bandits and RL (no \(\log T\) union), self-normalised bounds, sequential testing, change detection in non-stationary environments.

cards.name: Doob's maximal inequalities
cards.lay: For a (sub)martingale, the probability that the running maximum ever exceeds \(t\) up to time \(n\) is controlled by the value at time \(n\) alone. Lets you upgrade “bound at the end” to “bound along the whole path”.
cards.st: If \((M_k)_{k\le n}\) is a non-negative submartingale, then for \(t>0\): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\max_{k\le n}M_k\ge t\Bigr)\le\frac{{\mathbb{E}} M_n}{t},\qquad\Bigl\|\max_{k\le n}M_k\Bigr\|_p\le\frac{p}{p-1}{\lVert M_n\rVert}_p\ (p>1). \]
ver: Kolmogorov's inequality: for independent zero-mean \(X_i\), \(\Pr(\max_{k\le n}|S_k|\ge t)\le{\operatorname{Var}}(S_n)/t^2\).
Exponential maximal: apply to \(e^{\lambda M_k}\) to get maximal Azuma/Freedman bounds.
\(L^2\): \({\mathbb{E}}\max_{k\le n}M_k^2\le4{\mathbb{E}} M_n^2\).
cards.det: Proof idea. Let \(\tau=\min\{k:M_k\ge t\}\); then \(t\Pr(\tau\le n)\le{\mathbb{E}}[M_\tau{\mathbf{1}}\{\tau\le n\}]\le{\mathbb{E}}[M_n{\mathbf{1}}\{\tau\le n\}]\le{\mathbb{E}} M_n\) by the submartingale property.
cards.ex: If \(|D_t|\le c\) then \(\Pr(\max_{k\le n}S_k\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2nc^2)}\): the maximum of a bounded martingale over the whole horizon is as concentrated as its endpoint.
cards.use: Path-wise bounds in stochastic approximation (ODE method), uniform-in-time regret bounds, almost-sure convergence proofs.

cards.name: Law of the iterated logarithm & finite-time LIL bounds
cards.plain: Law of the iterated logarithm & finite-time LIL bounds
cards.lay: The running average of i.i.d. noise fluctuates, over infinitely many times, by about \(\sqrt{2\sigma^2\log\log n/n}\). Finite-time versions give confidence bounds valid for all \(n\) costing only a \(\log\log n\) (instead of \(\log n\)) penalty.
cards.st: (Khinchin's LIL) For i.i.d. \(X_i\) with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), almost surely \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2n\log\log n}}=1. \] (Finite LIL, e.g. Jamieson et al. 2014; Howard et al. 2021) For \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian increments, with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), simultaneously for all \(n\ge1\): \[ \frac{|S_n|}{n}\le C\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log\log(en)+\log(1/\delta)}{n}} \quad\text{for a universal constant } C. \]
ver: Stitching/peeling: apply a maximal inequality on epochs \([2^k,2^{k+1})\) with failure probability \(\delta/(k+1)^2\) and union bound.
lil'UCB for best-arm identification uses finite-LIL widths to achieve near-optimal sample complexity.
cards.det: Peeling argument: on epoch \(k\) (\(n\in[2^k,2^{k+1})\)), Doob/Azuma maximal bound with \(\delta_k=\delta/(k+1)^2\) gives width \(\sigma\sqrt{2\cdot2^{k+1}\log((k+1)^2/\delta)}\); since \(k\approx\log_2n\), this is \(\sqrt{n\log(\log n/\delta)}\) up to constants. The LIL shows the \(\log\log n\) cannot be removed.
cards.ex: Best-arm identification with fixed confidence: stopping rules based on finite-LIL bounds need \(O\bigl(\sum_a\Delta_a^{-2}\log(\log(1/\Delta_a)/\delta)\bigr)\) samples — matching lower bounds up to constants.
cards.use: Pure exploration, anytime algorithms, sequential testing, change detection thresholds.

cards.name: Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality
cards.lay: The empirical CDF is uniformly close to the true CDF: the worst-case gap over all thresholds is about \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\), with no dependence on the distribution. Useful for quantiles, CVaR and distributional RL.
cards.st: For i.i.d. real samples with CDF \(F\) and empirical CDF \(F_n\), for all \({\varepsilon}>0\) (Massart's tight constant): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\sup_x|F_n(x)-F(x)|>{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\le2e^{-2n{\varepsilon}^2}. \]
ver: One-sided: \(\Pr(\sup_x(F_n(x)-F(x))>{\varepsilon})\le e^{-2n{\varepsilon}^2}\) for \({\varepsilon}\ge\sqrt{\log2/(2n)}\).
Glivenko–Cantelli theorem: \(\sup_x|F_n-F|\to0\) a.s.
Consequence for risk measures: CVaR and quantiles of returns can be estimated uniformly at rate \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\) (times range).
cards.det: The class of half-lines has VC dimension 1 VC dimension & Sauer–Shelah lemma, so a uniform bound is expected; DKW gives the optimal constant. Note \(\sup|F_n-F|\) is the Kolmogorov distance; for distributions on \([a,b]\), Wasserstein-1 \(=\int|F_n-F|\le(b-a)\sup|F_n-F|\) Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality (Wasserstein-1).
cards.ex: Distributional RL with a generative model: the empirical return distribution of a fixed policy is within \({\varepsilon}\) in Kolmogorov distance after \(n\approx\log(2/\delta)/(2{\varepsilon}^2)\) rollouts.
cards.use: Risk-sensitive RL (CVaR, quantiles), distributional RL guarantees, quantile bandits.

cards.name: Bennett's inequality
cards.lay: A sharper version of Bernstein: uses the exact shape of the Poisson-like tail. Matters when variance is very small relative to the range (e.g. rare large rewards).
cards.st: Let \(X_i\) be independent, \(X_i-{\mathbb{E}} X_i\le b\), \(\sum_i{\operatorname{Var}} X_i\le v\). Then with \(h(u)=(1+u)\log(1+u)-u\): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\sum_i(X_i-{\mathbb{E}} X_i)\ge t\Bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{v}{b^2}h\Bigl(\frac{bt}{v}\Bigr)\Bigr). \]
ver: Since \(h(u)\ge\tfrac{u^2}{2(1+u/3)}\), Bennett implies Bernstein Bernstein's inequality.
For large \(u\), \(h(u)\approx u\log u\): tails decay like \(e^{-(t/b)\log(bt/v)}\), faster than exponential — Poisson regime.
cards.det: Proof: Chernoff Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method with the MGF bound \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le\exp\bigl(\tfrac{\sigma^2}{b^2}(e^{\lambda b}-1-\lambda b)\bigr)\), which follows from \(\tfrac{e^{x}-1-x}{x^2}\) being increasing.
cards.ex: Counting rare events: if each of \(n\) trials has success probability \(p\) (\(v\approx np\), \(b=1\)) then \(\Pr(\text{count}\ge np+t)\le\exp(-np\,h(t/(np)))\) — the Poisson tail.
cards.use: Sharp constants in variance-aware analyses, rare-event estimation, Poisson-like reward models.

cards.name: Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition
cards.lay: Some variables (squares of Gaussians, products, exponential waiting times) have heavier, exponential tails. They still concentrate, but with a two-regime tail: Gaussian for small deviations, exponential for large ones.
cards.st: \(X\) (mean \(\mu\)) is \(( u,\alpha)\)-sub-exponential if \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le e^{ u^2\lambda^2/2}\) for \(|\lambda|<1/\alpha\). Then \[ \Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp\Bigl(-\min\Bigl\{ rac{t^2}{2 u^2}, rac{t}{2\alpha}\Bigr\}\Bigr). \] For independent sub-exponential \(X_i\), \(\sum X_i\) is \((\sqrt{\sum u_i^2},\max\alpha_i)\)-sub-exponential.
ver: \(\psi_1\)-norm characterisation: \({\lVert X\rVert}_{\psi_1}=\inf\{K:{\mathbb{E}} e^{|X|/K}\le2\}\); \({\lVert XY\rVert}_{\psi_1}\le{\lVert X\rVert}_{\psi_2}{\lVert Y\rVert}_{\psi_2}\).
Chi-square: \(\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i^2\) satisfies \(\Pr(|\tfrac1n\sum Z_i^2-1|\ge t)\le2e^{-nt^2/8}\) for \(t\in(0,1)\) (Laurent–Massart give sharp versions).
cards.det: Bernstein's inequality is exactly the concentration of sums of sub-exponential variables. Appears when analysing squared errors (least-squares losses with sub-Gaussian noise), empirical covariance matrices, and products of features with noise.
cards.ex: Least-squares value estimation: the excess loss \((f(x)-y)^2-(f^\star(x)-y)^2\) with sub-Gaussian noise is sub-exponential; Bernstein-type fast rates follow.
cards.use: Fast rates for least squares (FQI, LSTD), covariance estimation, chi-square concentration in Gaussian lower bounds.

cards.name: Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp)
cards.lay: Sums of independent random matrices concentrate in operator norm much like scalar sums, with an extra \(\log d\) factor for the dimension. Used to show empirical feature covariances are well-conditioned.
cards.st: Let \(X_k\) be independent symmetric \(d\times d\) random matrices with \({\mathbb{E}} X_k=0\), \({\lVert X_k\rVert}\le L\), and \(\sigma^2={\lVert \sum_k{\mathbb{E}} X_k^2\rVert}\). Then \[ \Pr\Bigl(\Bigl\|\sum_kX_k\Bigr\|\ge t\Bigr)\le2d\exp\Bigl(-\frac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2+Lt/3}\Bigr). \]
ver: Matrix Chernoff (PSD summands \(0\preceq X_k\preceq LI\), \(\mu_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}(\sum{\mathbb{E}} X_k)\)): \(\Pr(\lambda_{\min}(\sum X_k)\le(1-{\varepsilon})\mu_{\min})\le d\bigl(\tfrac{e^{-{\varepsilon}}}{(1-{\varepsilon})^{1-{\varepsilon}}}\bigr)^{\mu_{\min}/L}\).
Rectangular matrices via the Hermitian dilation; matrix Freedman for martingales (Tropp 2011).
Covariance estimation: \({\lVert \widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\rVert}\lesssim{\lVert \Sigma\rVert}\bigl(\sqrt{\tfrac{r\log d}{n}}+\tfrac{r\log d}{n}\bigr)\) with \(r\) the effective rank.
cards.det: Proof via the matrix Laplace transform and Lieb's concavity theorem Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality. In offline linear RL, matrix concentration + Weyl Weyl's inequality (eigenvalue perturbation) shows \(\widehat\Sigma\succeq\Sigma/2\) once \(n\gtrsim\tfrac{L^2}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}\log\tfrac d\delta\).
cards.ex: Random features \(\phi_i\) with \({\lVert \phi_i\rVert}^2\le L\): \(\lambda_{\min}(\tfrac1n\sum\phi_i\phi_i^\top)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) w.h.p. once \(n\ge\tfrac{8L}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}\log\tfrac d\delta\) (matrix Chernoff).
cards.use: Offline RL with linear features, LSTD/FQI conditioning, experimental design, spectral methods.

cards.name: Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions
cards.lay: Any Lipschitz function of a standard Gaussian vector — no matter how high the dimension — is concentrated around its mean with dimension-free sub-Gaussian tails.
cards.st: (Tsirelson–Ibragimov–Sudakov) If \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_d)\) and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2\): \[ \Pr\bigl(f(X)-{\mathbb{E}} f(X)\ge t\bigr)\le e^{-t^2/(2L^2)}. \]
ver: Norms: \({\lVert X\rVert}_2\) concentrates around \(\sqrt d\) with \(O(1)\) fluctuations.
Log-Sobolev route (Herbst argument); analogous results for strongly log-concave measures.
Talagrand's convex-distance inequality for product measures Talagrand's convex-distance inequality.
cards.det: Important in high-dimensional and Gaussian lower-bound constructions; also gives concentration of the supremum of Gaussian processes around its mean, complementing Dudley Dudley's entropy integral (chaining).
cards.ex: \(\max_iZ_i\) (1-Lipschitz) concentrates within \(O(1)\) of \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iZ_i\approx\sqrt{2\log n}\).
cards.use: Gaussian process bandits, randomised value functions (RLSVI), high-dimensional lower bounds.

cards.name: Characterisations of convexity
cards.lay: A convex function lies above all of its tangent planes and below its chords. Equivalently, its Hessian is positive semidefinite. Local minima of convex functions are global, which is why convexity makes analysis easy.
cards.st: For differentiable \(f\) on a convex set, the following are equivalent: \[ egin{aligned}& ext{(i) } f( heta x+(1- heta)y)\le heta f(x)+(1- heta)f(y)\ \ orall heta\in[0,1];\ & ext{(ii) } f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle};\ & ext{(iii) } {\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y), x-y angle}\ge0.\end{aligned} \] If \(f\) is twice differentiable these are equivalent to \( abla^2f(x)\succeq0\).
ver: First-order optimality: \(x^\star\) minimises convex \(f\) over convex \(C\) iff \({\langle \nabla f(x^\star), y-x^\star\rangle}\ge0\) for all \(y\in C\).
Subgradients for non-smooth \(f\): \(f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle g, y-x\rangle}\) for \(g\in\partial f(x)\).
Operations preserving convexity: non-negative sums, pointwise sup (e.g. \(V^\star\) is convex in the reward vector \(r\)), composition with affine maps, partial minimisation.
Quasi-/pseudo-convexity and invexity are weaker notions; the policy-optimisation objective is non-convex but satisfies gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation.
cards.det: The value \(V^\pi(\rho)\) is not concave in policy parameters, but it is linear in the occupancy measure Discounted occupancy measures — so RL is a convex problem (an LP LP formulation of MDPs & its dual) in the right coordinates. Many “hidden convexity” results in policy optimisation exploit this.
cards.ex: \(V^\star(r)=\max_\pi{\langle d^\pi, r\rangle}/(1-\gamma)\) is a max of linear functions of \(r\), hence convex in \(r\) — used in inverse RL and robust reward analyses.
cards.use: Every optimisation argument; recognising hidden convexity (occupancy measures); subgradient methods for constrained MDPs.

cards.name: \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma
cards.lay: If a function's gradient doesn't change too fast (\(L\)-Lipschitz gradient), then it is sandwiched by quadratics, and a gradient step of size \(1/L\) is guaranteed to decrease it by \({\lVert \nabla f\rVert}^2/(2L)\). The starting point of every gradient-method analysis, including policy gradient.
cards.st: If \( abla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz then for all \(x,y\): \[ igl|f(y)-f(x)-{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle} igr|\le rac L2{\lVert y-x Vert}^2. \] Hence a gradient step \(x^+=x- frac1L abla f(x)\) satisfies \(f(x^+)\le f(x)- frac{1}{2L}{\lVert abla f(x) Vert}^2\).
ver: Non-convex rate: \(\min_{t<T}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le\tfrac{2L(f(x_0)-f^\star)}{T}\).
Convex \(+\) smooth: GD with step \(1/L\) gives \(f(x_T)-f^\star\le\tfrac{L{\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert}^2}{2T}\); Nesterov acceleration gives \(O(L{\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert}^2/T^2)\).

Co-coercivity (convex \(+\) smooth): \({\langle 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y), x-yangle}\ge	frac1L{\lVert 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)Vert}^2\).
Smoothness of the RL objective: for softmax policies, \(V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)\) is \(\tfrac{8}{(1-\gamma)^3}\)-smooth in \(\theta\) (Agarwal et al. 2021; Mei et al. 2020).
cards.det:
Proof: integral form of Taylor Taylor's theorem with remainder plus Cauchy–Schwarz: \(f(y)-f(x)-{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle}=\int_0^1{\langle abla f(x+t(y-x))- abla f(x), y-x angle}{\mathrm{d}} t\le\int_0^1Lt{\lVert y-x Vert}^2{\mathrm{d}} t\).

For policy gradient, smoothness alone gives only convergence to stationary points; global optimality needs gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation.
cards.ex: Softmax PG with exact gradients and step \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/8\): by the descent lemma \(V^{(t+1)}\ge V^{(t)}+\tfrac{\eta}{2}{\lVert \nabla V^{(t)}\rVert}^2\), so values increase monotonically; combining with the non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequality gives \(O(1/t)\) rates (Mei et al. 2020).
cards.use: Policy-gradient convergence, actor–critic analyses, gradient-EM, any GD/SGD proof.

cards.name: Strong convexity, PL & quadratic growth
cards.lay: Strongly convex functions curve upward at least quadratically, so they have a unique minimiser and gradient descent converges linearly. The weaker Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition — gradient large whenever you are far from optimal in value — is enough for linear rates and holds for some non-convex problems.
cards.st: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if \(f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle \nabla f(x), y-x\rangle}+\tfrac\mu2{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\). \(f\) satisfies \(\mu\)-PL if \[ \tfrac12{\lVert \nabla f(x)\rVert}^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^\star\bigr)\quad\forall x. \] If \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-PL, GD with step \(1/L\) gives \(f(x_t)-f^\star\le(1-\mu/L)^t(f(x_0)-f^\star)\).
ver: Strong convexity \(\Rightarrow\) PL \(\Rightarrow\) quadratic growth \(f(x)-f^\star\ge\tfrac{\mu}{2}\mathrm{dist}(x,X^\star)^2\) (with constants).
Strong convexity w.r.t. a general norm: negative entropy is \(1\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_1\) on the simplex (Pinsker Pinsker's inequality is equivalent to this!).

Strongly convex \(\Rightarrow\) \({\lVert x-x^\starVert}\le	frac1\mu{\lVert 
abla f(x)Vert}\) and \({\langle 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y), x-yangle}\ge\mu{\lVert x-yVert}^2\) (strong monotonicity).
Gradient domination in RL Gradient domination for policy optimisation is a (non-uniform) PL-type inequality.
cards.det:
Linear-rate proof under PL: descent lemma gives \(f(x_{t+1})-f^\star\le f(x_t)-f^\star-\tfrac{1}{2L}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le(1-\tfrac\mu L)(f(x_t)-f^\star)\).

In EM theory, strong concavity of \(Q(\cdot\mid\theta^\star)\) (Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu's \(\lambda\)-strong concavity condition) is exactly what makes the population EM operator a contraction Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction.
cards.ex: Entropy-regularised RL: adding \(\tau\mathcal H(\pi)\) makes the problem strongly concave in the right geometry; regularised NPG converges linearly at rate \((1-\eta\tau)^t\) (Cen et al. 2021).
cards.use: Linear convergence of regularised policy optimisation, EM contraction conditions, strongly convex regularisers in FTRL/OMD, fast rates in online learning (logarithmic regret).

cards.name: Gradient domination for policy optimisation
cards.lay: Even though the RL objective is non-convex in the policy, every stationary point is globally optimal (for direct parameterisation), because the suboptimality is bounded by how much a policy could still improve along the gradient — scaled by a distribution-mismatch factor.
cards.st: (Agarwal, Kakade, Lee, Mahajan 2021) For direct policy parameterisation and any start distribution \(\mu\), \[ V^\star(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\le\Bigl\|\frac{d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}{\mu}\Bigr\|_\infty\max_{\bar\pi}\bigl(\bar\pi-\pi\bigr)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)\cdot\frac{1}{1-\gamma}, \] where \({\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\) is the distribution-mismatch coefficient.
ver: Softmax parameterisation (Mei et al. 2020) — non-uniform Łojasiewicz: \({\lVert \nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(\mu)\rVert}_2\ge\tfrac{\min_s\pi_\theta(a^\star(s)|s)}{\sqrt S\,{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/d^{\pi_\theta}_\mu\rVert}_\infty}(V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho))\).
Linear-quadratic regulators: the LQR cost is gradient dominated in the gain \(K\) (Fazel et al. 2018).
Proof backbone: performance difference lemma Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) + pushing \(\max_a A^\pi(s,a)\) through the mismatch ratio.
cards.det: By the PDL, \(V^\star-V^\pi=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi^\star}A^\pi(s,a)\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}\max_aA^\pi(s,a)\). Change measure to \(d^\pi_\mu\) using the mismatch coefficient, and recognise \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi_\mu}\max_aA^\pi\) as \((1-\gamma)\max_{\bar\pi}(\bar\pi-\pi)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)\). Hence a policy with small “projected gradient” is near-optimal.
cards.ex: Projected gradient ascent on the simplex with step \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/(2\gamma|{\mathcal{A}}|)\) finds an \({\varepsilon}\)-optimal policy in \(O\bigl(\tfrac{|{\mathcal{S}}||{\mathcal{A}}|}{(1-\gamma)^6{\varepsilon}^2}{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}^2_\infty\bigr)\) iterations.
cards.use: Global convergence of policy gradient methods, actor–critic theory, LQR policy gradient, understanding why exploration (via \(\mu\)) matters for PG.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

cards.name: Convex conjugate & Fenchel–Young
cards.lay: The conjugate \(f^*\) describes a convex function by its supporting lines (slope \(\mapsto\) intercept). It turns maximisation problems into dual problems and produces variational formulas — e.g. log-sum-exp is the conjugate of negative entropy, KL is the conjugate of the log-MGF.
cards.st: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is \(f^*(y)=\sup_x\{{\langle x, y\rangle}-f(x)\}\). It is always convex, \(f^{**}=f\) for closed convex \(f\) (Fenchel–Moreau), and \[ {\langle x, y\rangle}\le f(x)+f^*(y)\quad\text{(Fenchel--Young)},\quad\text{with equality iff }y\in\partial f(x). \]
ver: Negative entropy on the simplex \(f(p)=\sum p_i\log p_i\) has \(f^*(y)=\log\sum_ie^{y_i}\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
\(f(x)=\tfrac12{\lVert x\rVert}^2\Rightarrow f^*(y)=\tfrac12{\lVert y\rVert}_*^2\); \(f(x)=\tfrac1p|x|^p\Rightarrow f^*(y)=\tfrac1q|y|^q\) (Young Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul)).
Duality of smoothness/strong convexity: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) iff \(f^*\) is \(\tfrac1\mu\)-smooth w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_*\).
Fenchel duality: \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\ge\sup_y\{-f^*(-A^\top y)-g^*(y)\}\), with equality under constraint qualification.

Legendre transform of the log-MGF gives the Chernoff rate function Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method; Donsker–Varadhan is a conjugate-duality statement Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle.
cards.det: Conjugate duality explains: (i) why regularised RL has softmax optimal policies (\(\nabla\)LSE \(=\) softmax); (ii) why FTRL with regulariser \(R\) plays \(\nabla R^*(-\eta\sum\ell)\); (iii) the dual LP for MDPs; (iv) variational formulas for divergences \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations used in GAIL/IRL and in off-policy estimation (DualDICE).
cards.ex: Soft Bellman backup: \(\max_{\pi(\cdot|s)}\{{\langle \pi, Q(s,\cdot)\rangle}+\tau\mathcal H(\pi)\}=\tau\log\sum_ae^{Q(s,a)/\tau}\), attained at \(\pi\propto e^{Q/\tau}\).
cards.use: Entropy-regularised RL, FTRL/OMD, Lagrangian duality, variational divergence estimation, DICE-family off-policy estimators.

cards.name: Projection theorem & non-expansiveness of projections
cards.lay: Onto a closed convex set, every point has a unique closest point, and projecting two points never increases their distance. This is why projected gradient methods and projected Bellman operators behave well.
cards.st: Let \(C\) be nonempty closed convex in a Hilbert space. Then \(\Pi_C(x)={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{y\in C}{\lVert x-y\rVert}\) exists, is unique, and is characterised by \({\langle x-\Pi_C(x), y-\Pi_C(x)\rangle}\le0\) for all \(y\in C\). Moreover \[ {\lVert \Pi_C(x)-\Pi_C(y)\rVert}\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}. \]
ver: Pythagorean inequality: \({\lVert y-\Pi_C(x)\rVert}^2+{\lVert \Pi_C(x)-x\rVert}^2\le{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\) for \(y\in C\).

Subspaces: \(\Pi\) is linear and self-adjoint; weighted projections \(\Pi_D\) onto span\((\Phi)\) in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) are used in TD Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy).
Bregman projections satisfy a generalised Pythagorean inequality Bregman divergences & the three-point identity.
cards.det: In projected gradient descent the analysis \({\lVert x_{t+1}-x^\star\rVert}^2\le{\lVert x_t-\eta g_t-x^\star\rVert}^2\) uses non-expansiveness with \(x^\star\in C\). For TD with linear function approximation, the projected Bellman operator \(\Pi_DT^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) because \(\Pi_D\) is non-expansive in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) and \(T^\pi\) is a contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) when \(D\) is the stationary distribution Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy).
cards.ex: Projection onto the probability simplex can be computed in \(O(n\log n)\) by sorting; used in projected policy gradient with direct parameterisation.
cards.use: Projected gradient methods, TD with linear function approximation, constrained policy optimisation.

cards.name: Lagrangian duality & Slater's condition
cards.lay: Constrained problems can be turned into unconstrained min–max games by pricing the constraints with multipliers. The dual problem always gives a bound (weak duality) and, for convex problems with a strictly feasible point, the bound is tight (strong duality). This is the foundation of constrained MDPs.
cards.st: For \(\min_xf(x)\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le0\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_ig_i(x)\) and \(D(\lambda)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda)\). Then \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0}D(\lambda)\le f^\star\) (weak duality). If \(f,g_i\) are convex and some \(x\) has \(g_i(x)<0\) for all \(i\) (Slater), then \[ \max_{\lambda\ge0}D(\lambda)=f^\star. \]
ver: Constrained MDPs: \(\max_\pi V_r^\pi\) s.t. \(V_g^\pi\ge b\) has zero duality gap (Altman 1999; Paternain et al. 2019) because it is an LP in occupancy measures — even though it is non-convex in \(\pi\).
Saddle point characterisation: \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\) optimal iff it is a saddle point of \(L\).
Bound on the optimal multiplier under Slater: \({\lVert \lambda^\star\rVert}_1\le\tfrac{f(\bar x)-f^\star}{\min_i(-g_i(\bar x))}\) — crucial for primal–dual CMDP regret.
cards.det: Primal–dual algorithms for CMDPs alternate policy updates on \(L(\pi,\lambda)=V_r^\pi+\lambda(V_g^\pi-b)\) with (projected) gradient steps on \(\lambda\). The multiplier bound keeps \(\lambda\) in a known box, which is needed to bound the dual regret.
cards.ex: CMDP with Slater slack \(\xi\) (\(V_g^{\bar\pi}\ge b+\xi\)): \(\lambda^\star\le\tfrac{V_r^\star-V_r^{\bar\pi}}{\xi}\le\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)\xi}\).
cards.use: Constrained/safe RL, primal–dual policy optimisation, LP duality for MDPs, entropy/KL-regularised formulations.

cards.name: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions
cards.lay: At an optimum of a constrained problem, the gradient of the objective is balanced by a non-negative combination of the active constraint gradients. For convex problems these conditions are also sufficient — they let you guess and verify optimal solutions.
cards.st: For \(\min f(x)\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le0\), \(h_j(x)=0\) (under a constraint qualification), an optimum \(x^\star\) admits \(\lambda\ge0, u\) with \[ abla f(x^\star)+\sum_i\lambda_i abla g_i(x^\star)+\sum_j u_j abla h_j(x^\star)=0,\quad\lambda_ig_i(x^\star)=0,\quad g_i(x^\star)\le0,\ h_j(x^\star)=0. \]
ver: For convex problems with Slater's condition, KKT is necessary and sufficient.
Simplex constraint example: maximising \({\langle p, q\rangle}+\tau\mathcal H(p)\) over \(p\in\Delta\) gives \(p_i\propto e^{q_i/\tau}\).
Water-filling, maximum-entropy distributions, and the M-step of EM for mixtures (\(\pi_k=\tfrac1n\sum_i\gamma_{ik}\)) are all KKT solutions.
cards.det: Complementary slackness (\(\lambda_ig_i=0\)) is what makes the dual LP of an MDP pick out optimal actions: the dual variables (occupancies) are positive only on actions where the Bellman inequality is tight.
cards.ex: M-step for mixture weights: maximise \(\sum_k n_k\log\pi_k\) s.t. \(\sum\pi_k=1\); KKT gives \(n_k/\pi_k=\nu\), so \(\pi_k=n_k/n\).
cards.use: Deriving closed-form M-steps, regularised policy updates, LP complementary slackness for MDPs, constrained RL.

cards.name: Minimax theorems (von Neumann, Sion)
cards.lay: In a zero-sum game with convex–concave payoff (e.g. mixed strategies), it does not matter who moves first: \(\min\max=\max\min\). Used for games, robust RL, Lagrangian duality and Yao's principle in lower bounds.
cards.st: (Sion) Let \(X\) be compact convex, \(Y\) convex, \(f(x,y)\) convex and lsc in \(x\), concave and usc in \(y\). Then \[ \min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y). \] (von Neumann) For a matrix \(A\): \(\min_{p\in\Delta_m}\max_{q\in\Delta_n}p^\top Aq=\max_q\min_pp^\top Aq\).
ver: Weak inequality \(\sup\min\le\min\sup\) always holds (no assumptions).
Markov games: Shapley's theorem — the minimax value exists and satisfies a contracting Bellman equation Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\).
Yao's principle: worst-case expected cost of the best randomised algorithm \(=\) best deterministic algorithm against the worst input distribution — basis of lower bounds.
No-regret dynamics: if both players run sublinear-regret algorithms, average play converges to the minimax value at rate \(({\mathrm{Reg}}_1+{\mathrm{Reg}}_2)/T\).
cards.det: Minimax lower bounds in learning theory, \(\inf_{\text{alg}}\sup_{\text{env}}{\mathbb{E}}[\text{loss}]\), are typically lower bounded by switching to a Bayesian prior over environments (sup \(\ge\) average), which is the easy direction of the minimax theorem.
cards.ex: Robust MDP with \((s,a)\)-rectangular uncertainty sets: \(\max_\pi\min_{P\in{\mathcal{P}}}V^\pi_P=\min_P\max_\pi V^\pi_P\), and the robust Bellman operator is a contraction.
cards.use: Markov games, robust RL, adversarial training (GAIL), primal–dual analysis, lower bounds via Yao's principle, no-regret learning in games.

cards.name: Bregman divergences & the three-point identity
cards.lay: A Bregman divergence measures how far a convex function is above its tangent: it generalises squared Euclidean distance (and KL divergence) and obeys a “law of cosines” that makes mirror descent analyses telescope.
cards.st: For strictly convex differentiable \(\psi\): \(D_\psi(x,y)=\psi(x)-\psi(y)-{\langle abla\psi(y), x-y angle}\ge0\). For all \(x,y,z\): \[ {\langle abla\psi(z)- abla\psi(y), x-z angle}=D_\psi(x,y)-D_\psi(x,z)-D_\psi(z,y)\quad ext{(three-point identity)}. \]
ver: \(\psi=\tfrac12{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2^2\Rightarrow D_\psi(x,y)=\tfrac12{\lVert x-y\rVert}^2\); \(\psi(p)=\sum p_i\log p_i\) on the simplex \(\Rightarrow D_\psi(p,q)={\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality.
Generalised Pythagoras: for Bregman projection \(z={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{u\in C}D_\psi(u,y)\), \(D_\psi(x,y)\ge D_\psi(x,z)+D_\psi(z,y)\) for all \(x\in C\).
Exponential families: \(D_A(\theta',\theta)={\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta'})\) where \(A\) is the log-partition function.
If \(\psi\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\): \(D_\psi(x,y)\ge\tfrac\mu2{\lVert x-y\rVert}^2\).
cards.det: The three-point identity is the single line that powers mirror descent Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma, NPG/policy mirror descent Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence, and the mirror-descent view of EM EM as minorise–maximise and as mirror descent. It is proved by simply expanding the three divergences.
cards.ex: KL three-point identity on the simplex: \({\langle \log\tfrac{p_{t+1}}{p_t}, p^\star-p_{t+1}\rangle}={\mathrm{KL}}(p^\star\|p_t)-{\mathrm{KL}}(p^\star\|p_{t+1})-{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{t+1}\|p_t)\) — the core step of Hedge and NPG analyses.
cards.use: Mirror descent / NPG / policy mirror descent, Hedge, EM as mirror descent, Bregman projections in online learning, exponential-family statistics.

cards.name: Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma
cards.lay: Mirror descent takes gradient steps in a geometry tailored to the constraint set (e.g. multiplicative updates on the simplex). Its regret is (initial divergence)/\(\eta\) + \(\eta\times\)(sum of squared gradient norms in the dual norm). Natural policy gradient is mirror descent per state.
cards.st: Let \(\psi\) be \(1\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) on \(C\) and \(x_{t+1}={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{x\in C}\{\eta{\langle g_t, x\rangle}+D_\psi(x,x_t)\}\). Then for any \(u\in C\): \[ \sum_{t=1}^T{\langle g_t, x_t-u\rangle}\le\frac{D_\psi(u,x_1)}{\eta}+\frac\eta2\sum_{t=1}^T{\lVert g_t\rVert}_*^2. \]
ver: Entropic MD on the simplex \(=\) Hedge: \({\langle g_t, x_t-u\rangle}\) regret \(\le\tfrac{\log n}{\eta}+\tfrac\eta2\sum_t{\lVert g_t\rVert}_\infty^2\) Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound.
Euclidean MD \(=\) projected OGD Online gradient descent regret (Zinkevich).
Local-norm refinement (for non-negative losses with entropy): \(\le\tfrac{\log n}{\eta}+\eta\sum_t\sum_ix_{t,i}g_{t,i}^2\) — key for EXP3 EXP3 & importance-weighted loss estimators.

Policy mirror descent: \(\pi_{k+1}(\cdot|s)\propto\pi_k(\cdot|s)e^{\eta Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)}\) is OMD in each state with linear losses \(-Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)\) Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence.
cards.det: Proof. Optimality of \(x_{t+1}\) gives \({\langle \eta g_t+\nabla\psi(x_{t+1})-\nabla\psi(x_t), u-x_{t+1}\rangle}\ge0\). Apply the three-point identity Bregman divergences & the three-point identity, then bound \(\eta{\langle g_t, x_t-x_{t+1}\rangle}-D_\psi(x_{t+1},x_t)\le\tfrac{\eta^2}{2}{\lVert g_t\rVert}_*^2\) by Young Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul) and strong convexity. Telescope Telescoping sums.
cards.ex: With \(n\) experts and losses in \([0,1]\): \(\eta=\sqrt{2\log n/T}\) gives regret \(\le\sqrt{2T\log n}\).
cards.use: Natural policy gradient / PMD convergence, adversarial MDPs (O-REPS), Hedge/EXP3, online learning in non-stationary environments, game dynamics.

cards.name: Stochastic gradient descent convergence
cards.lay: With unbiased noisy gradients, SGD on convex problems converges at rate \(1/\sqrt T\) (or \(1/T\) under strong convexity). Non-convex smooth problems reach stationary points at rate \(1/\sqrt T\) in gradient norm squared. The template for stochastic policy gradient and TD analyses.
cards.st: Let \(f\) be convex, \({\mathbb{E}}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial f(x_t)\), \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert g_t\rVert}^2\le G^2\), \({\lVert x_1-x^\star\rVert}\le D\). With \(\eta=\tfrac{D}{G\sqrt T}\) and averaged iterate \(\bar x_T\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} f(\bar x_T)-f^\star\le\frac{DG}{\sqrt T}. \]
ver: \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\eta_t=\tfrac{1}{\mu t}\): \({\mathbb{E}} f(\bar x_T)-f^\star=O\bigl(\tfrac{G^2\log T}{\mu T}\bigr)\) (or \(O(G^2/(\mu T))\) with suffix/weighted averaging).

\(L\)-smooth non-convex, variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\eta\asymp\min(1/L,1/(\sigma\sqrt T))\): \(\min_t{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2=O\bigl(\tfrac{L\Delta}{T}+\tfrac{\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta}}{\sqrt T}\bigr)\), \(\Delta=f(x_1)-f^\star\).
High-probability versions via Azuma/Freedman on the martingale \(\sum_t{\langle \nabla f(x_t)-g_t, x_t-x^\star\rangle}\).
Markovian noise (as in TD/actor–critic): rates degrade by a mixing-time factor Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.
cards.det: Proof: same telescoping argument as OGD Online gradient descent regret (Zinkevich) applied in expectation, followed by Jensen on the average. Equivalent to online-to-batch conversion Online-to-batch conversion of the OGD regret.
